docs.title: MapwiseFox
docs.text:
MapwiseFox is a suite of tools for building and running systematic literature reviews: searching multiple academic databases with a single query, deduplicating and screening results, and tracking evidence through a review pipeline.

New to the repo? Start with Getting Started for the workspace-wide setup (cloning, uv sync, shared .env conventions).

Each tool in the suite is documented here:

  • Search — search multiple databases at once with a CLI backed by a single DSL that compiles down to vendor-specific query syntax for ACM, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, Scopus, Springer, and Web of Science.
  • Deduplication — merge records from several sources and group duplicate papers into one reviewable workbook.
  • Split — divide study workbooks into screening bundles or independent evaluation assignments for your reviewers.
  • Snowballing — expand a set of known papers by following their references or citations through Semantic Scholar, with Excel workbooks as input and output.
  • Metrics — measure search retrieval quality and agreement between screening or quality-assessment raters.
  • Assistant — use large language models to support study selection and quality assessment against your criteria.
  • Web — import an Excel primary-study list, screen evidence in a browser, and track include or exclude decisions.

Contributing tool documentation is highly encouraged.

docs.title: 10StepsinExcelforWoS: Streamlining bibliometric analysis in web of science using Microsoft excel
docs.text:
Tsair-Wei Chien a, Willy Chou b,c,*

a Department of Medical Research, Chi Mei Medical Center, Tainan, Taiwan

docs.title: A R T I C L E I N F O
docs.text: Keywords: Bibliometric analysis Web of science Excel VBA Data wrangling Visualization framework

docs.title: A B S T R A C T
docs.text: Numerous bibliometric studies utilize professional software to generate visualizations from specialized text files downloaded from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC). However, when using Microsoft Excel (MS Excel) files exported from WoSCC, researchers often face a series of manual and cumbersome data preprocessing tasks that hinder efficiency. To address this challenge, this study proposes a streamlined framework—10StepsinExcelforWoS—to facilitate bibliometric analysis using MS Excel. A total of 1719 articles published in the journal of SoftwareX between 2017 and 2025 were retrieved from WoSCC. The proposed method involves 10 sequential steps implemented via Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) within Excel to wrangle the data. Two types of visualizations were demonstrated: (1) a summary report for performance analysis and (2) Kano and Sankey diagrams to identify dominant entities in bibliometric research since 2017. Key findings identified the United States as the leading country; Delft University of Technology (Netherlands) as the top institution; the Department of Computer Science as the most prevalent affiliation—appearing across 60 uni versities for first authors and 42 for corresponding authors; Wojciech Salabun (Poland) as the most prolific author; and “MODEL” as the most prominent keyword.This study concludes that the 10StepsinExcelforWoS offers a practical, transparent, efficient, and reproducible workflow for conducting nuanced bibliometric analyses directly in MS Excel.

docs.title: 1. Motivation and significance
docs.text:
In recent years, bibliometric analysis has become a cornerstone in evaluating academic productivity, research trends, and scholarly impact across disciplines [1]. While professional tools like CiteSpace[2], VOSviewer[3], and Bibliometrix[4] are widely adopted to generate visualizations from standardized text files exported from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC)[5], their functionality often relies on specific file formats and predefined workflows. In contrast, Excel-exported

WoSCC files, although widely accessible, typically require laborious manual preprocessing steps before they can be used for in-depth bib liometric research(e.g., publications [1,6–8] that rely on the R platform [9]). These steps include data filtering, field standardization, metadata restructuring, and summary table generation—tasks that are both time-consuming and prone to inconsistency, especially for novice users.

docs.title: 1.1. Research gaps in current bibliometric workflows
docs.text:
Despite the maturity of bibliometric software, several gaps remain in the practical workflow for researchers aiming to use Excel-based outputs:

(1) Lack of streamlined preprocessing for Excel data: Researchers often face tedious, repetitive operations when attempting to clean and structure raw Excel data from WoSCC, which hinders reproducibility and deters early-career scholars.

(2) Insufficient integration of VBA-based automation: Few studies leverage Microsoft Excel’s scripting capabilities (i.e., Visual Basic for Applications, VBA) to automate and simplify these bibliometric tasks.

(3) Limited reproducible frameworks for non-specialists: Most bibliometric tools require some level of software familiarity (e.g., Java, R, Python), which creates a barrier for users with limited programming backgrounds. Moreover, the non-transparency of the data source will hinder the reproducibility of some corre sponding studies [10].

(4) Ranking only for metadata elements: Traditional bibliometric methods rely on frequency-based rankings, lacking analytical depth. The underused dominance coefficient (DC) [11,12] can quantify gaps between top-ranked elements.

docs.title: 1.2. Addressing the practical needs of bibliometric researchers
docs.text:
Exploring graphs (e.g., slope, summary report, or other charts) is crucial for researchers, as they offer a clearer view of complex temporal relationships in bibliometric data [1]. For example, adopting slope graphs enhances the interpretability of time-series data, improves trend identification, and conveys comparative dynamics more effectively. However, methods for extracting core elements are based on sufficient data collected with datasets (e.g., those in MS Excel).That is, the quality and accuracy of those graph visualizations depend heavily on rigorous data wrangling prior to analysis.

Bibliometric data exported from databases like WoSCC often contain inconsistencies, duplicates, and unstructured metadata across key variables such as publication year, affiliation, and keywords [10]. Without proper cleaning, restructuring, and filtering, the input data may lead to misleading or cluttered visualizations. Therefore, data wrangling is a foundational step to ensure that only statistically relevant and compa rably formatted elements are fed into visualization tools like slope graphs, ultimately enabling more precise and meaningful insights into scholarly trends over time. Likewise, data wrangling before conducting performance analysis of metadata entities is essential to ensure the generation of reliable and interpretable summary reports. However, the technique of ’data mugging’—the systematic extraction and restructuring of key bibliometric fields—has received limited attention in previous studies [1].

To close these gaps, there is a pressing need for a lightweight, transparent, and reproducible Excel-based framework that facilitates bibliometric analysis without depending on complex software environments. Such a solution would be especially valuable in educational settings or for interdisciplinary researchers who may not have access to specialized bibliometric platforms.

docs.title: 1.3. Challenges of reproducibility and transparency in bibliometric studies
docs.text:
Previous bibliometric case studies have struggled with reproduc ibility and transparency due to incomplete disclosure of data-processing steps and opaque workflows. As Liu [10] noted, reporting “Web of Science Core Collection” without specifying subsets (e.g., SCI-Expanded, SSCI), coverage years, or search date undermines reproducibility. Moreover, database-focused studies document concrete inconsistencies that can bias results, including coverage/indexing differences across WoS and Scopus; incomplete or erroneous funding acknowledgments; missing/ambiguous author–affiliation links; document-type and Early Access mislabeling; uneven identifier coverage (ORCID/ResearcherID); and variable availability of abstracts, Author Keywords, and Keywords Plus [13–18].

To address these issues, our framework operationalizes a transparent, auditable pipeline: (i) record full data provenance (database, subsets, years, search date); (ii) normalize authors, affiliations, docu ment types, Early Access, and keyword fields; (iii) de-duplicate primarily by DOI (with title-based fallback); (iv) log every transformation; and (v) perform analyst-supervised identity checks that combine full names with affiliation/country, using ORCID where available. The workflow is implemented in Excel/VBA (“10StepsinExcelforWoS”) and integrates DC analysis [11,12], thereby standardizing wrangling, strengthening quality control, and improving reproducibility.

docs.title: 1.4. Study goal and contribution
docs.text:
This study proposes a novel framework titled 10StepsinExcelforWoS (or ExcelWoS for short), which utilizes a 10-step VBA-powered process in Microsoft Excel (MS Excel) to streamline bibliometric data wrangling, visualization, and performance reporting. The method was applied to analyze articles indexed in WoSCC. Two types of visual outputs were generated:

(1) a summarized performance report [1] based on ten key met adata elements, and

(2) Kano and Sankey diagrams [1,19–21] to identify dominant countries in bibliometric publishing.

By validating this Excel-based approach, the study aims to enhance the transparency, accessibility, and reproducibility of bibliometric research. The framework also responds to growing demands for simplified tools that support nuanced academic insights.

This study aims to evaluate whether a structured, VBA-powered Excel workflow—implemented through the 10StepsinExcelforWoS framework—can generate bibliometric visualizations and performance analyses that are comparable in clarity and analytical value to those produced by specialized software, while offering improved accessibility, usability, and reproducibility.

docs.title: 2. Software description
docs.text: To streamline bibliometric analysis using MS Excel, this study developed a standardized 10-step “ExcelWoS” framework. This approach employs VBA to automate data wrangling, performance summarization, and visualization tasks for records exported from the database of WoSCC.

docs.text:
Before creating the summary report, author-made MS-Excel module [22] and instruction with MP4 video[23] can be downloaded and viewed on the R-platform[9].

docs.title: 2.1.2. Five steps for extracting data from WoSCC
docs.text:
The following steps outline the procedure for extracting and orga nizing data exported from WoSCC using the downloaded Excel tool [22]:

  1. Insert Journal Impact Factors: Ensure that the Journal Impact Factors (e.g., from Journal Citation Reports: Impact Factor List 2025 [24]) are deposited in Sheet1 of the spreadsheet.

  2. Rename Downloaded Files Using R: Use the provided R script to rename all Excel files downloaded into the wos folder. This ensures consistent naming for batch processing [25].

  3. Set File Path and Verify File List: Open the designated Excel file (e. g., named data) and set the file path to:

C:\Users\user\Downloads\wos\

Confirm that the renamed file names are listed vertically from cell A2 downward.

  1. Activate VBA Import: Click the “From WoS in folder” macro button. This will trigger the VBA automation process to import data from each listed file.

  2. Consolidate Data into ALL Worksheet: In the “ddd” worksheet, click the icon labeled “Paste data into All in AG.” This action automatically transfers and consolidates the imported data into the ALL worksheet, ready for further data wrangling and analysis.

docs.title: 2.1.3. Keywords from keyplus to top 10 using R script
docs.text: The R script [26] was applied to obtain top 10 keywords pasted to the spreadsheet of author at the cell of A82 downward.

docs.title: 2.2. Software functionalities and steps for implementing excelwos
docs.text: To emphasize the importance of reproducibility in bibliometric research [27], we parsed the WoSCC Excel export fields (e.g., Authors, Affiliations, Countries), in which multiple entries are separated by semicolons (;). Using the split function in MS Excel VBA, we also marked special tokens such as the corresponding author and their affiliation details (e.g., Mengist, W (corresponding author)).

docs.title: 2.2.2. Ten steps for arranging data in MS excel
docs.text:
1. Import data: Transfer content from cell AG1 to A1 in the ALL spreadsheet.

  2. Extract metadata categories: Use the Country field in the ALL spreadsheet to extract metadata categories.

  3. Calculate CJAL score: Compute the CJAL score using the provided metrics [28,29].

  4. Extract metadata each: Collect all relevant metadata (e.g., keywords and KeyPlus) into the spreadsheet.

  5. Obtain Top 10 elements: In the author spreadsheet, retrieve the top 10 elements for each metadata entity.

  6. Compute h-index by category: In column Y, calculate the h index for each metadata category (excluding keywords).

  7. Overall h-index: Refer to cell author!AD94 for the overall hindex across all articles.

  8. Calculate CJAL score for keywords: Use rows 82 to 91 in the keyword section to calculate the CJAL score for each keyword [28,29].

  9. Keyword-specific h-index: Use columns V82 to Y82 to compute the h-index [30] for each keyword.

  10. Read summary report: Click on the spreadsheet titled “10descriptionmap” to view the final summary report.

docs.title: 2.3,1. R platform for visuals using Kano and Sankey diagrams
docs.text:
It is recommended to use visual coding scripts [31] for generating Kano and Sankey diagrams, utilizing a CSV file (e.g., country.csv) containing keyword co-occurrence data. The resulting Kano diagram categorizes entities into four quadrants: Leader, Lone Wolf, Follower, and Coworker. Classification is based on the Dominance Coefficient (DC) [11,12], which quantifies relative influence. Leadership strength is further divided into five tiers: Super $( \mathrm { D C } \ge 0 . 8 )$ , Quasi-Super $( \mathrm { D C } \geq 0 . 7 ) ,$ Strong $( \mathrm { D C } \geq 0 . 6 )$ , Moderate $( \mathrm { D C } \geq 0 . 5 ) _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , and Weak $( \mathrm { D C } < 0 . 5 )$ [32]. As such, incorporating DC with KD [19,21] (or Sankey diagram[1]) enhances clarity by illustrating dominance or imbalance across metadata entities, offering more insightful bibliometric evaluation.

Based on structured reports suggested by authors [1], the findings were presented in two subsections: (1) Performance Analysis Findings and (2) Visualization Outputs.

docs.title: 2.3.2 R package used in this study
docs.text: Visualizations in R created on the R platform [31] were used to draw Kano and Sankey diagrams. All data processing and statistical analyses were conducted using R software version 4.1.3 [33], and the generation of time-series visualizations and result output was performed within the RStudio integrated development environment [34].

docs.title: 3.1. Data source
docs.text:
In line with recommendations by Liu [10], we explicitly disclose the details of the dataset used in this study. Articles were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC), including both the Science Citation Index Expanded (SCI-Expanded) and the Social Sciences Citation Index (SSCI). The coverage period was from 2017 to 2025, with the search conducted on July 29, 2025. By specifying both the subsets and the temporal coverage, this study ensures full transparency and facilitates reproducibility for future bibliometric investigations.

These articles were retrieved to identify leading metadata categories and verify the study hypothesis. Study data are deposed in Github [35]. Since all articles stored in WoSCC do not contain identifiable patient

docs.title: 3.2.1 Performance analysis findings
docs.text:
Fig. 2 displays a performance summary report outlining major contributors and corresponding counts across ten key metadata categories in bibliometric research from 2017 to 2025. The analysis incorporates metrics such as the number of publications by corresponding authors (RP), first authors (FP), h-index values [30], and DC scores [11,12]. In total, 1719 articles were analyzed, with an overall h-index of 48.

Key insights drawn from the performance report include the leading contribution of United States, with Delft Univ Technol (Netherlands) as the most prolific institution, and the Department of Computer Science as the most frequently listed organizational affiliation. Wojciech Salabun from Poland emerged as the most productive author, and SoftwareX as the most common journal as expected. Other dominant attributes include the year 2024, the document type "Article", the Department of Computer Science as the most prevalent affiliation—appearing across 60 universities for first authors and 42 for corresponding authors, and the most frequent keyword “MODEL” Notably, the most cited pub lication—a 2018 article by Susi Lehtola(U.S)—received 551 citations.

Among all top-performing entities, only the document type "Article" achieved a DC score above 0.70 (DC = 0.99), suggesting that no other entity held a clearly dominant position (i.e., >0.7) within its respective category during the study period.

docs.title: 3.2.2 Visualization outputs
docs.text:
Author collaborations and co-keyword occurrences were clustered using Follower-Leading Clustering algorithm(FLCA) [1,21,36]. Top 20 elements were selected and shown on either Kano or Sankey diagram. United States (Fig. 3) emerges as a strong leader with a DC of 0.60.

In contrast, Politecn Torino(Italy) is not classified as a leader (Fig. 4) due to limited collaborative influence in the field, while the keyword “MODEL” (Fig. 5) represents a strong leader (DC = 0.61).

docs.title: 3.4. To tests the study hypothesis
docs.text: The findings of this study confirm that a structured, VBA-driven Excel workflow—implemented through the ExcelWoS framework—can successfully generate bibliometric visualizations and performance analyses that are comparable in clarity and analytical value to those (e.g., shown in Table 1) produced by any specialized bibliometric software, while providing enhanced accessibility, usability, and reproducibility for researchers, as shown in author-made MS-Excel module [22] and instruction with MP4 video [23].

docs.title: 4. Impact
docs.text:
The ExcelWoS tool introduces a new capability in bibliometric research by automating data wrangling for downstream analysis—a function not available in any of the 10,248 PubMed-indexed bibliometric studies to date [36]. This transition from manual data handling to automated resolution with ExcelWoS unlocks several novel research avenues. For example, researchers can now analyze disciplinary characteristics by article category with clear and concise bibliometric outputs [1], and make comparisons across institutions or countries—task that previously required cumbersome tables and graphs.

ExcelWoS significantly advances the pursuit of existing bibliometric questions by enhancing both the granularity and automation of the datawrangling process. In contrast to traditional tools such as VOSviewer [3], Bibliometrix [4], and CiteSpace [2], which lack built-in data preparation capabilities, ExcelWoS integrates FLCA-based clustering [1, 37] alongside Kano and Sankey diagram visualizations [1,19,20,32]. This integration streamlines bibliometric workflows and minimizes the need for manual curation.

In practice, ExcelWoS has already facilitated the extraction of extensive metadata for downstream analyses. The accompanying R scripts [9] are designed for user-friendliness, allowing researchers without advanced programming expertise to conduct bibliometric analyses efficiently. Early adopters [1,6–8] have reported significant reductions in metadata preparation time and enhanced clarity in translating metadata into a structured format. ExcelWoS for future

ExcelWoS fills a critical gap in bibliometric methodology by providing an accessible, user-friendly tool for metadata wrangling. Thi enhancement streamlines the analytical process, thereby accelerating scholarly discovery and supporting more effective institutional knowledge management.

A notable strength of this study is its proactive handling of WoSCC metadata limitations. While previous research has identified inconsistencies and biases in key fields [10], we implemented systematic cleaning of author information, consistency checks for publication and citation data, and validation across multiple metadata categories. These steps improved data reliability and interpretability, transforming what is often a source of limitation into a methodological strength.

docs.title: 5. Conclusion
docs.text:
This study introduces ExcelWoS, a lightweight yet powerful VBAdriven framework that addresses critical gaps in bibliometric work flows, particularly for researchers relying on Excel-exported data from WoSCC. By automating ten essential steps—including data wrangling, performance reporting, and visualization—ExcelWoS enhances the reproducibility, accessibility, and interpretability of bibliometric analyses. It integrates advanced features such as FLCA clustering and dominance coefficient (DC) scoring, producing insightful visual outputs like summary reports, Kano diagrams, and Sankey diagrams.

As a transparent and reproducible framework, ExcelWoS offers strong potential for integration into institutional dashboards, library systems, and future SaaS platforms. Ultimately, ExcelWoS democratizes bibliometric analysis, streamlines scholarly evaluation, and opens new avenues for trend discovery and academic decision-making.

docs.title: A R T I C L E I N F O
docs.text: Keywords: Bibliometric software WoSCC metadata Visualization framework AAC metric Web-based application

docs.title: A B S T R A C T
docs.text:
Numerous bibliometric studies rely on specialized software to visualize Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) metadata, but direct, reproducible workflows for standard 72-column XLS files remain limited. We developed App4WoSCCinR, a web-based framework that enables users to upload WoSCC metadata and execute bibliometric analysis through a simple two-step process. Using SoftwareX articles published between 2017 and March 2026 as an illustrative dataset, the application generated a structured performance summary and visual outputs across countries, institutions, departments, authors, journals, keywords, and temporal trends. It also incorporates the Absolute Advantage Coefficient (AAC) to identify dominant entities within bibliometric networks. The demonstration showed that App4WoSCCinR can efficiently transform standard WoSCC metadata into interpretable summaries and visual analytics for research evaluation. Overall, the framework provides a practical and transparent solution for low-barrier bibliometric analysis directly from WoSCC spreadsheet exports.

● A web-based tool, App4WoSCCinR, was developed for streamlined bibliometric analysis from standard 72- column WoSCC metadata.

● The framework produced a summary report and over 100 visualizations across 10 metadata domains, incorporating AAC to quantify dominance.

● Analysis of 2,061 SoftwareX articles demonstrated the tool’s practical value for transparent, efficient, and reproducible bibliometric workflows.

docs.title: 1. Motivation and significance
docs.text:
Bibliometric analysis has become an important approach for evalu ating research productivity, identifying emerging trends, mapping knowledge structures, and assessing scholarly impact across disciplines [1–3]. Widely used tools such as CiteSpace [4], VOSviewer [5], and Bibliometrix [6] enable visualization from standardized Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) data [7].However, these tools typically require specific input formats and predefined workflows, limiting flexibility when working with commonly available 72-column Excel-exported WoSCC files.

Fig. 1. Homepage of App4WoSCCinR illustrating the two-step workflow.

In practice, such 72-column files often require extensive manual preprocessing—including data cleaning, field standardization, and restructuring—before meaningful analysis can be conducted [8–12]. These steps are time-consuming, error-prone, and hinder reproduc ibility, particularly for users without programming expertise.

docs.title: 1.1. Existing tools and remaining workflow challenges
docs.text:
A mature software [4–6,13] ecosystem already supports such work with plain text files for non-coders. Reviews of bibliometric software have shown that these tools vary in scope, with different strengths in performance analysis, science mapping, preprocessing, visualization, and user accessibility [14].

Recent developments have further expanded this ecosystem. For example, BibexPy [15] was introduced as a preprocessing-oriented tool for merging WoSCC and Scopus data, DOI-based deduplication, and metadata enrichment, while BiblioMerge [16] was designed to support merging, duplicate removal, author normalization, and compatibility with downstream bibliometric programs. These developments show that important progress has already been made in automating bibliometric workflows, especially for data integration and cleaning.

Nonetheless, the availability of multiple tools does not eliminate a practical workflow challenge for many users(i.e., it still requires moving across several steps from exporting records and cleaning metadata to generating publication-ready Figures [17]. Even when robust tools are available, the overall process may remain fragmented for users who prefer a direct upload-and-run workflow on commonly downloaded spreadsheet files rather than multi-stage scripting or tool chaining. A practical need therefore remains for an integrated, accessible workflow that enables bibliometric visualization directly from WoSCC Excel metadata.

docs.title: 1.2. Practical need for direct and reproducible WoSCC workflows
docs.text:
WoSCC [7] remains one of the most widely used sources for bibliometric research because it indexes journals, conference proceedings, and books across a broad range of disciplines [15,16]. WoSCC records can be exported to spreadsheet formats, which are convenient for users but may still require cleaning, normalization, restructuring, or format conversion before consistent downstream analysis. Related guidance and workflow papers likewise emphasize the importance of combining and cleaning bibliometric data before visualization and interpretation [8].

This issue is not simply technical; it also affects accessibility and reproducibility. Code-based environments offer high flexibility, but users without programming experience may find preprocessing and multi-tool orchestration burdensome. Conversely, graphical tools may reduce the coding burden but still differ in import expectations, field handling, export options, or output types. Taken together, these workflow-level constraints suggest the value of a low-barrier framework that can accept a standard WoSCC export, perform core preprocessing steps transparently, and generate repro ducible bibliometric outputs within a single environment.

Additionally, reproducibility remains a major concern in bibliometric research. Many studies lack detailed reporting of data sources, including WoSCC subsets, coverage periods, and search dates, limiting replicability [18]. Furthermore, inconsistencies across databases—such as incomplete author–affiliation links, misclassified document types, and uneven identifier coverage—can introduce bias [19–24] on following visualizations.

docs.title: 1.3. Study goal and scope
docs.text:
To address this practical need, we developed App4WoSCCinR [25], a browser-based framework designed for users who want to move directly from a WoSCC spreadsheet export to automated bibliometric summaries and visual outputs with minimal manual intervention. In the current implementation, the platform is organized around a simple two-step workflow—data upload and automated execution—and produces both a structured summary report and a large set of exportable visualizations across multiple metadata domains.

Using articles indexed in WoSCC for SoftwareX as an illustrative case, the present study demonstrates how App4WoSCCinR supports metadata preprocessing, performance analysis, and Figure generation within a unified web workflow. The emphasis is therefore on implementation, usability, and reproducible output generation, while positioning the software as a practical complement to the existing bibliometric tool

Fig. 2. System architecture and workflow of App4WoSCCinR, showing the transformation of WoSCC spreadsheet input into normalized intermediate tables, domain level summary statistics, visualization outputs, and exportable reports.

ecosystem.

docs.title: 1.4. Contribution of the present work
docs.text:
The contribution of App4WoSCCinR lies in workflow integration and accessibility. Specifically, the framework emphasizes: (1) direct handling of WoSCC spreadsheet exports; (2) minimal manual preprocessing; (3) browser-based execution; (4) automatic generation of structured summary panels and diverse visualization outputs in a single run; (5) and AAC-enhanced dominance [26,27] reporting as a comple mentary layer beyond simple counts and rankings.

In this sense, the novelty of the software is practical rather than exclusive: it packages several otherwise separate steps into a streamlined web interface intended for transparent and reproducible biblio metric analysis.

docs.title: 2. Software description
docs.text:
App4WoSCCinR [25] is a web-based bibliometric analysis frame work developed to process standard 72-column WoSCC metadata and generate both structured summary reports and multi-domain visualization outputs within a unified workflow.

The software is designed to reduce manual preprocessing and to support reproducible bibliometric analysis through a streamlined upload-and-run interface. Beyond the user-facing simplicity of the platform, the system is organized as a modular analytical pipeline that separates data ingestion, metadata normalization, indicator computation, visualization rendering, and export.

docs.title: 2.1. System architecture and workflow
docs.text:
The architecture of App4WoSCCinR consists of five major modules:

(1) input parsing,

(2) metadata cleaning and normalization,

(3) domain-wise aggregation and indicator computation,

(4) visualization rendering, and

(5) export and report generation.

The overall workflow begins with the upload of a WoSCC spreadsheet file (.xls or .xlsx) or the provision of a valid URL pointing to bibliometric data.

The imported records are parsed into an internal tabular structure and then passed to preprocessing routines that clean, standardize, and restructure key metadata fields. The normalized outputs are subsequently converted into domain-specific summary tables, which are used to compute bibliometric indicators and generate the final visualizations and summary report. The resulting outputs can then be displayed in the web interface or exported as image and archive files.

The two-step workflow (Fig. 1) —data upload and automated execution—serves as the entry point to a deeper modular backend that transforms raw WoSCC spreadsheet metadata into publication-ready Figures.

docs.title: 2.2. Modular design
docs.text: Five modules are involved in App4WoSCCinR, as shown in Fig. 2.

docs.title: 2.2.1. Module 1: Input parsing
docs.text:
The input module accepts WoSCC metadata in spreadsheet form and supports both local file upload and URL-based loading. A demonstration dataset is also provided for rapid testing and illustration. Regardless of input source, all datasets are processed through the same parsing logic so that subsequent analytical steps remain consistent.

The software validates the file format, reads the raw worksheet content, checks that the imported structure is compatible with WoSCC style metadata, and converts the records into a standard internal data frame for downstream processing.

docs.title: 2.2.2. Module 2: Metadata cleaning and normalization
docs.text:
The second module performs metadata preprocessing, including trimming, delimiter harmonization, missing-value handling, and restructuring of multi-value fields such as authors, affiliations, and keywords. This step is necessary because WoSCC spreadsheet exports, although convenient for users, often require normalization before consistent bibliometric analysis can be performed.

The preprocessing routines generate structured intermediate tables suitable for domain-level aggregation. For example, author, institution, department, country, and keyword fields are split, standardized, and transformed into countable analysis units. This module therefore acts as the bridge between raw WoSCC metadata and analysis-ready bibliometric objects.

docs.title: 2.2.3. Module 3: Domain-wise aggregation and indicator computation
docs.text:
After normalization, the third module constructs summary tables across major metadata domains, including 10 metadata doamins. For each domain, the software computes bibliometric indicators such as publication count and h-index, and applies the Absolute Advantage Coefficient (AAC) [26,27] to quantify the relative dominance of leading entities.

By separating aggregation from preprocessing, the software allows multiple visual outputs to be generated from the same standardized intermediate data rather than repeatedly transforming the original spreadsheet. This design improves consistency, efficiency, and trace ability across outputs.

docs.title: 2.2.4. Module 4: Visualization rendering
docs.text:
The rendering module converts domain-level summary tables into graphical outputs. In the current implementation, App4WoSCCinR produces more than 100 visualizations spanning multiple metadata domains. These include summary plots[8], slope graphs, chord diagrams [28], Sankey-style relationship displays[29], Slope graphs[30], SSplot [31], world maps, regional maps for China and the United States, and Lotka-related author productivity displays.

Different metadata structures are routed to different rendering functions. Temporal summaries are used to generate slope plots[30]; relational or co-occurrence data are used in chord and network-based displays; geographic tables are passed to map functions; and clustered data are used to construct SSplots[31]. This modular rendering approach allows the platform to support heterogeneous visualizations within a single analytical environment.

docs.title: 2.2.5. Module 5: Export and report generation
docs.text:
The final module assembles the outputs into downloadable artifacts.

A structured summary report is generated to present key contributors and bibliometric indicators across metadata domains, while individual Figs. can be exported as PNG files. In addition, a ZIP package of outputs can be downloaded to support reuse, sharing, and reproducibility.

This module ensures that App4WoSCCinR functions not only as an exploratory interface but also as a reporting tool capable of producing reusable materials for bibliometric research and presentation.

docs.title: 2.3. Implementation layers
docs.text:
From an implementation perspective, App4WoSCCinR can be viewed as four interacting layers:

(1) a front-end Shiny interface,

(2) a server-side preprocessing layer,

(3) an analytical engine, and

(4) a Figure/Report export layer.

The front-end interface manages file upload, URL input, execution, preview, and downloading. The server-side preprocessing layer handles raw-data parsing and metadata normalization. The analytical engine computes domain-level summaries and bibliometric indicators, including AAC-based dominance [26,27] reporting. The rendering and export layer then transforms these intermediate results into Figures and downloadable reports.

This layered design clarifies that the two-step user workflow is intentionally simple, whereas the software itself implements a structured backend pipeline for bibliometric data transformation and output generation.

docs.title: 2.4. Representative code logic
docs.text: To improve readability and reproducibility, the representative implementation is now presented as formatted R code listings. The native R pipe operator |> passes the output of the expression on its left to the function on its right, allowing sequential data-processing steps to be written clearly.

docs.title: 2.4.1. WoSCC field parsing
docs.text:
The parser imports the uploaded WoSCC spreadsheet, standardize column names, and trims character fields before downstream processing.

raw <- readxl::read_excel(input$file$datapath)
raw <- raw |>
  dplyr::rename_with(trimws) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(
      where(is.character),
      trimws
    )
  )

docs.title: 2.4.2. Author and affiliation normalization
docs.text:
Multi-value metadata fields are separated into atomic units so that authors, affiliations, keywords, and related WoSCC fields can be counted consistently.

author_tbl <- raw |>
  dplyr::select(AU) |>
  tidyr::separate_rows(AU, sep = ";") |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    AU = stringr::str_squish(AU)
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(AU != """)

The same normalization strategy is applied to affiliations, keywords, countries, and other multi-value metadata fields. This ensures that summary tables are derived from standardized analytical units rather than raw spreadsheet strings.

summary_tbl <- author_tbl |>
  dplyr::count(AU, sort = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::rename(
    entity = AU,
    n = n
  )
summary_tbl <- add_h_index(summary_tbl)
summary_tbl <- add_aac(summary_tbl)

docs.title: 2.4.3. AAC-based dominance computation
docs.text: After domain-level counts are generated, App4WoSCCinR appends summary indicators, including the h-index [32] and AAC [8,26,27,33], to identify dominant entities within each bibliometric domain. The following listing illustrates author-level summarization.

docs.title: 2.5. AAC used to determine dominant strength over the next two elements
docs.text:
The AAC was used to quantify the dominance strength of the leading entity relative to the next two ranked entities. Let $ u _ { 1 } , u _ { 2 } ,$ , and $ u _ { 3 }$ denote the observed values of the first-, second-, and third-ranked entities, respectively.

The dominance ratio was calculated as $r = ( u _ { 1 } / u _ { 2 } ) / ( u _ { 2 } / u _ { 3 } )$ , and the AAC was then computed as $A A C = r / ( 1 + r )$ . Thus, AAC transforms the dominance ratio into a bounded coefficient between 0 and 1.

A higher AAC indicates stronger dominance of the leading entity over its nearest competitors, whereas a lower AAC suggests a more even distribution among the top-ranked entities. App4WoSCCinR provides an AAC dashboard to support visual interpretation of dominance patterns across bibliometric domains (Fig. 1) [33].

docs.title: 2.6. Multi-panel output generation
docs.text:
Domain-specific tables are routed to plotting functions and then assembled into exportable outputs.

p1 <- render_summary_plot(country_tbl)

p2 <- render_slope_plot(year_tbl)

p3 <- render_chord_plot(collab_tbl)

p4 <- render_ssplot(keyword_tbl)

export_plots(list(p1, p2, p3, p4), outdir = tempdir())

These examples are intended to illustrate the internal logic of the framework rather than to reproduce the full application code.

docs.title: 2.7. Repository structure
docs.text: The repository is organized to reflect the modular architecture of the software. Core scripts and functions are grouped into components for input handling, metadata preprocessing, analytical summarization, AAC computation, visualization generation, and export. This structure helps readers identify the major implementation units responsible for parsing WoSCC data, constructing domain summaries, rendering Figures, and packaging outputs.

docs.title: 2.8. User-facing workflow and functionalities
docs.text:
At the interface level, App4WoSCCinR provides a simplified two-step workflow(Fig.1):

  1. Upload WoSCC data

  2. Users may either upload a WoSCC file (.xls/.xlsx) or provide a valid URL to bibliometric data, using the passcode 5730687835; a demo dataset is also available for rapid testing without a passcode.

  3. Run analysis

  4. By clicking the analysis function, the system automatically performs preprocessing, summary computation, and visualization rendering in real time.

The main output functions include:

• Report, which generates a structured summary of bibliometric performance;

• Slope, which displays temporal publication trends;

• Chord, which visualizes inter-entity relationships;

docs.title: 2.9.1. R code for visualization and reporting
docs.text:
App4WoSCCinR was implemented on shiny.io[34] to support auto mated bibliometric visualization and reporting from standard 72-col umn WoSCC metadata.

The framework integrates data preprocessing, metadata summarization, and visual output generation within a unified workflow. Rather than relying solely on single-purpose scripts for individual plots, this study used modular R code to produce a summary report and multiple visualization outputs across key metadata domains, including country, institution, department, author, journal, year, document type, discipline, keyword, and region.

In this study, the generated outputs included summary plots, temporal trend plots, chord diagrams, Sankey diagrams, SSplots, geographic maps, and other bibliometric visualizations.

Following the reporting structure suggested in previous bibliometric studies [8,30], the results were organized into two parts: (1) performance analysis findings and (2) visualization outputs.

docs.title: 2.9.2. R code used in this study
docs.text:
All data processing, visualization, and statistical analyses were conducted using R version 4.3.3 [35]. The application was developed and tested in the RStudio integrated development environment [36]. Core functions were written to automate metadata cleaning, restruc turing, summary reporting, dominance analysis, and Figure generation, thereby allowing users to complete bibliometric analysis through a simple upload-and-run web interface.

The code base supports reproducible generation of publication indicators, AAC-based rankings, and over 100 visualizations from WoSCCexported metadata, as deposited in Github [37]. Instruction with MP4 video[38] and An example of url link [39] to App4WoSCCinR are presented.

docs.title: 3.1. Data source
docs.text: Articles published in SoftwareX were retrieved from WoSCC, including both the Science Citation Index Expanded (SCI-Expanded) and the Social Sciences Citation Index (SSCI). The coverage period was from 2017 to 2026, with the search conducted on March 20, 2026. By specifying both the subsets and the temporal coverage, this study ensures full transparency and facilitates reproducibility for future bibliometric investigations. Study data are deposited in Github [31] and Supplemental Appendix 1, with buttons of Browse and Run WoS to show visualizations in Fig. 1 .

docs.title: 3.2.2. Visualization outputs
docs.text:
App4WoSCCinR generates a world map in Fig. 3 showing publication counts by country, alongside a chord diagram illustrating international collaboration patterns among major contributing countries.

The Fig. 4 displays yearly publication counts for the top contributing countries identified from WoSCC metadata. Red lines connect annual publication counts to illustrate longitudinal growth patterns. The United States demonstrated the highest and most sustained publication activity, whereas countries such as Spain, Poland, and China exhibited rapid increases in recent years. The visualization highlights dynamic shifts in international research productivity over time.

Keywords were clustered using the FLCA. Colored bars represent cluster membership, whereas AAC values indicate dominance of the leading keyword within each cluster. Silhouette scores (SS) and modularity-related indicators are shown on the right to evaluate cluster cohesion and separation. Higher AAC and SS values indicate stronger thematic dominance and more stable cluster structures.

docs.title: 3.3. Reaching the study goals
docs.text:
This study achieves the study goals that a streamlined web-based framework, implemented through App4WoSCCinR, can effectively (1) perform bibliometric analysis from standard 72-column WoSCC Excel metadata and (2) generate outputs with substantial analytical value.

As shown in Table 3, the practical contribution of App4WoSCCinR is not to replace established science-mapping tools, but to provide an integrated, low-barrier workflow that accepts standard WoSCC Excel exports directly and generates structured summary reporting plus diverse visual outputs within a single web-based execution environment.

Through its two-step workflow—data upload and automated analysis—the system produced both a structured performance summary and over 100 visualizations across multiple metadata domains.

These findings demonstrate that App4WoSCCinR is capable of sup porting bibliometric interpretation in a manner that is clear, efficient, and reproducible. In particular, the integration of the AAC [8,20,21,24, 27] enabled more nuanced identification of dominant entities than simple frequency rankings alone.

The proposed framework thus meets the study goal of providing a practical and transparent alternative for bibliometric analysis, especially for users seeking low-barrier and reproducible analytical tools.

docs.title: 4. Impact
docs.text:
App4WoSCCinR extends the earlier 10StepsinExcelforWoS framework [8] into a visualization-oriented bibliometric platform capable of processing standard 72-column WoSCC spreadsheet metadata through a browser-based workflow. By integrating metadata ingestion, preprocessing, structured reporting, AAC-enhanced dominance analysis, and multi-domain visualization within a single environment, the platform reduces manual preprocessing requirements and lowers technical barriers for bibliometric exploration.

Compared with established tools such as CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and Bibliometrix, the contribution of App4WoSCCinR lies primarily in workflow integration and direct handling of native WoSCC spreadsheet metadata rather than replacement of existing science-mapping software. The framework emphasizes rapid upload-and-run processing together with exportable structured summaries and diverse visualization outputs across countries, institutions, authors, journals, keywords, and temporal trends.

The inclusion of AAC [8,26,27,36] provides a complementary dominance-oriented indicator that extends conventional frequency-based summaries by quantifying the relative strength of leading entities compared with nearby competitors.

App4WoSCCinR also improves transparency of bibliometric preprocessing by documenting metadata normalization and structured aggregation workflows. This is particularly relevant because WoSCC metadata may contain inconsistencies such as incomplete affiliations, author-name ambiguity, inconsistent document-type labeling, and incomplete keyword coverage in historical records [40]. Although these issues cannot be fully eliminated by downstream software, deterministic preprocessing and normalization procedures can improve interpretability and reproducibility.

Several limitations should be addressed. First, the current imple mentation primarily supports WoSCC-derived metadata and does not yet provide direct interoperability with Scopus, Dimensions, or OpenAlex formats. Second, preprocessing outcomes may still be influenced by metadata incompleteness, author-disambiguation ambiguity, and database-specific indexing practices. Third, formal scalability bench marking for very large bibliometric datasets has not yet been systematically evaluated. These limitations remain important directions for future development and validation.

docs.title: 5. Conclusion
docs.text: App4WoSCCinR offers a practical web-based framework for analyzing standard 72-column WoSCC metadata through a simple twostep workflow. By generating structured reports, diverse visualizations, and AAC-based dominance indicators without programming, it improves accessibility, transparency, and reproducibility for efficient bibliometric analysis.

docs.title: Deploying an Interactive Machine Learning System in an Evidence-Based Practice Center: abstrackr
docs.text:
Byron C. Wallace†‡, Kevin Small‡, Carla E. Brodley†

Joseph Lau‡, Thomas A. Trikalinos‡

†Tufts University, Medford, MA

‡Tufts University and Tufts Medical Center, Boston, MA byron.wallace@gmail.com, kevin.small@gmail.com, brodley@cs.tufts.edu jlau1@tuftsmedicalcenter.org, ttrikalinos@tuftsmedicalcenter.org

docs.title: ABSTRACT
docs.text: Medical researchers looking for evidence pertinent to a specific clinical question must navigate an increasingly voluminous corpus of published literature. This data deluge has motivated the development of machine learning and data mining technologies to facilitate eficient biomedical research. Despite the obvious labor-saving potential of these technologies and the concomitant academic interest therein, however, adoption of machine learning techniques by medical researchers has been relatively sluggish. One explanation for this is that while many machine learning methods have been proposed and retrospectively evaluated, they are rarely (if ever) actually made accessible to the practitioners whom they would benefit. In this work, we describe the ongoing development of an end-to-end interactive machine learning system at the Tufts Evidence-based Practice Center. More specifically, we have developed abstrackr, an online tool for the task of citation screening for systematic reviews. This tool provides an interface to our machine learning methods. The main aim of this work is to provide a case study in deploying cutting-edge machine learning methods that will actually be used by experts in a clinical research setting.

docs.title: Categories and Subject Descriptors
docs.text:
I.2.1 [Artificial Intelligence]: Applications and Expert Systems—Medicine and science General Terms Software, Human Factors Keywords

machine learning, active learning, medical, applications, text classification, evidence-based medicine

docs.title: 1. INTRODUCTION AND MOTIVATION
docs.text:
The appeal of machine learning in the context of the biomedical domain is obvious: there are not enough human experts to organize and make sense of the exponentially increasing volume of published scientific literature, and it therefore makes sense to attempt to reduce the burden on experts with computational methods. Indeed, methodological and empirical studies of machine learning techniques applied to biomedical data abound [13]. Yet despite the potential benefits of such methods, they are rarely deployed in practice.

This article describes ongoing work on a deployed interactive machine learning system that aims to reduce the burden on researchers undertaking systematic reviews. A systematic review is an exhaustive (usually quantitative) assessment of all of the published medical evidence relevant to a precisely formed clinical question. Conducting such reviews requires reviewers (usually physicians) to search literature repositories (e.g., PubMed) to retrieve all potentially eligible citations (comprising titles and abstracts). They then must wade through this pool, designating each citation as eligible or not, based on their criteria. This process is known as citation screening, and it is the bane of many systematic reviewers. In a typical review, the initial PubMed query might produce around 5,000 potentially eligible citations, and all of these must be evaluated to find the ∼250 (∼5%) that will ultimately be deemed eligible.

Our objective is to mitigate this workload, i.e., reduce the burden imposed on researchers during the citation screening phase of systematic reviews. Citation screening can be re-cast as a classification task in which the aim is to induce a model to classify documents as ‘relevant’ or ‘irrelevant’ to the question/criteria at hand. Indeed, there have been a few studies that have demonstrated the potential of classification techniques for this task [12]. Further, we have previously demonstrated the additional utility of allowing the domain experts (reviewers) to interact with the machine learning system. More specifically, the citation screening task is an ideal candidate for active learning (AL), in which the classifier is trained interactively by the domain expert in order to make better use of the latter’s time (we describe this at greater length in Section 2). Additionally, domain experts in clinical research bring a wealth of background knowledge to their task, and it makes sense to exploit this knowledge to build a better model with less efort; to this end, we use the dual supervision paradigm [1], which allows experts to specify that certain features (in the case of text, words or ngrams) correlate with classes (e.g., ‘relevant’ or ‘irrelevant’ citations).

As a practical means of deploying the aforementioned machine learning techniques, we have developed the abstrackr tool.1 abstrackr is a collaborative (i.e., multiple reviewers can simultaneously screen citations for a review), web-based annotation tool for the citation screening task. It evolved from our original, prototypical stand-alone desktop annotation tool developed for citation screening [10]; the previous version was not collaborative (primarily because it was not web-based), and it did not have the capability to directly integrate active learning. Even without the machine learning components, abstrackr in its current form has been found useful by researchers at the Tufts Evidence based Practice Center (EPC), where it is currently being routinely used. This is an added benefit for a few reasons. First, having real users provides a springboard for experimenting with novel interactive learning protocols, such as active learning. Second, because they are already using the tool, the eventual tighter integration with the machine learning technologies will be seamless from their perspective. We also note that for a few reviews, we have used classification techniques prospectively to reduce workload.

docs.title: 2. ACTIVE LEARNING AND DUAL SUPER-VISION
docs.text: We now discuss a few emerging interactive paradigms in machine learning that can help with the citation screening task by making better use of the reviewer’s time, i.e., these methods can produce a better classification model with less human efort. In Section 3, we discuss how the abstrackr tool facilitates these techniques.

docs.title: 2.1 Active Learning
docs.text:
In the canonical supervised machine learning scenario, it is assumed that the learner is given a training set of labeled instances from which a model is to be induced; its performance will then be assessed on the remaining instances (the test set). The assumption is that the instances comprising the training set were selected at random. By contrast, active learning (AL) (see [6] for a survey) allows the learning algorithm to select which instances are to comprise its training set. The hope is that by allowing the learning algorithm to select the instances that the expert is to label, rather than selecting these at random, a better model can be induced with less annotation efort (i.e., fewer labels).

Generally, AL methods define a function mapping a given unlabeled instance xi (e.g., an unread citation) to a scalar encoding, roughly, the expected value of acquiring a label for x , in terms of inducing a classifier. All of the unlabeled instances are then ranked by this criterion in descending order, thereby prioritizing for annotation those instances that are likely to best inform the classification model. The aim is to build a better model with fewer (informative) labels, as opposed to randomly sampling training data, which may result in wasting the expert’s time by asking him or her to label uninformative instances. Perhaps the most popular AL strategy is uncertainty sampling, in which the classifier requests from the expert a label for the unlabeled instance about whose class membership it is least certain [9].

AL has consistently performed well in experimental settings, particularly for text classification [9]. Furthermore, we have elsewhere demonstrated the potential utility of AL for the citation screening task specifically [10]. Nonetheless, there are questions regarding its eficacy in practice [3, 7, 2].

An under-appreciated obstacle to deploying AL systems in the ‘real-world’ is confronting the unrealistic assumptions typically made in AL research [4, 11]. In particular, it is usually assumed that there is a single, infallible, oracular expert who will provide accurate labels at a fixed cost. In our case, however, there are typically multiple reviewers participating in a given project, with varying levels of expertise (fallibility) and cost. We recently proposed a strategy for active learning in this scenario [11]: the idea is to assign the majority of labeling tasks to novice reviewers, who tend to be cheaper, and reserve more experienced (expensive) reviewers for ambiguous (i.e., dificult to classify) citations. More precisely, this is accomplished by relying on the metacognitive abilities of novice reviewers: we ask them to flag ambiguous/dificult citations as such, and re-assign these to more experienced experts. In the following section we will discuss how we are operationalizing this strategy with the abstrackr tool.

docs.title: 2.2 Dual Supervision
docs.text:
Classification algorithms in machine learning have historically been designed to learn from instance labels, i.e., classifiers are typically induced over a set of examples (e.g., biomedical citations) that have been manually categorized into the classes to which they belong. This is referred to as supervised learning. However, it has recently been observed by the machine learning community that alternative forms of supervision, e.g., indicating that a certain feature is associated with a particular class, may increase learning eficiency.

Indeed, when we first began experimenting with prospective active learning at the Tufts EPC, reviewers would express frustration that the model was ‘missing’ that, for example, they were uninterested in clinical trials that included children. Intuitively, experts should be able to communicate such information to the model by saying, for example, “if the word ‘children’ is in the abstract, then the citation should probably be excluded.” Dual supervision aims to achieve exactly this.

Various models for exploiting these feature-labels, once they are attained, have been proposed in the literature. These include active learning strategies [11, 7] and general classifier induction algorithms [5, 8]. The important point here is that an annotation tool that will ultimately feed into a classification algorithm should exploit this information if it’s available, as it is in the citation screening case.

docs.title: 3. INTRODUCING ABSTRACKR
docs.text:
Our goal in developing abstrackr has been to develop a practical means of putting the emerging machine learning technologies discussed above to semi-automate citation screening. This tedious screening task was previously being conducted by printing out reams of abstracts to read one by one while keeping track of labels in a spreadsheet. As one might imagine, this was a messy and generally unenjoyable endeavor, and because of this abstrackr has been found useful as a stand-alone annotation tool, independent of the machine learning components. In our case we thus have had domain experts willing to use the software, which has provided rapid feedback and empirical data with which to experiment with novel machine learning techniques.

The typical work-flow in abstrackr proceeds as follows. First, a literature search is conducted in the typical way, e.g.

Figure 1: A screenshot of the web-based ABSTRACKR tool. Terms that the expert has designated as indicative of relevance or irrelevance are highlighted. Users may enter additional terms into the textbox at the bottom of the screen, designating them as relevant (irrelevant) or strongly relevant (irrelevant) by clicking the single and double thumbs up (down) buttons, respectively. These labeled terms will ultimately be exploited by our learning algorithm, which integrates labeled term information into the popular SVM classification algorithm [8]. The reviewer can elect to accept (X), designate as borderline/ambiguous (?), or reject (×) the current citation. Once they do so, the next citation (as ordered by the active learning ordering function) will immediately be retrieved and displayed to the user.

Figure 2: The architecture of the ABSTRACKR system. See text for details.

via PubMed. Once the set of potentially eligible citations is retrieved, it is imported into abstrackr. A user accomplishes this by starting a new review/project in the system; to this end, they can upload either a list of PubMed IDs (these can be exported directly from the PubMed interface), an XML file exported from RefMan.2 or a tab-delimited file. The user who creates a review is designated as its lead. During the review creation process, the lead is asked a few questions regarding the project. In particular, they will be asked in which order citations are to be prioritized for screening – here they are specifying the AL function to be used. For example, they may elect to screen citations in order of the likelihood that they are relevant, as predicted by the current model, or by a criterion that ranks citations by the labeled terms (words/n-grams) that have been provided by the reviewers thus far. They may also elect to simply screen the citations in a random order. Once the review is created, the lead can invite other reviewers to join the project.

The primary interaction that a review participant has with the system is depicted in Figure 1. The user is presented with a citation (title, abstract and keywords) and can designate it as ‘relevant’, ‘borderline’ or ‘irrelevant’. Once one of these labels is assigned to the citation, the reviewer is immediately presented with a new citation to screen; this is the AL step. Which of the remaining unlabeled citations the system presents to the user is a function of the AL strategy being employed for the corresponding review. Note that terms or n-grams the user has labeled are highlighted in a color indicating their polarity, i.e., whether (and to what degree) the highlighted term is indicative of ‘relevance’ or ‘irrelevance’. Initial interactions with reviewers suggested that it is natural for them to provide two levels of granularity in either direction, i.e., a given term might be designated as ‘highly’ or ‘weakly’ indicative of relevance (irrelevance). Users can add additional labeled terms at the bottom of the page; the thumb icons correspond to the aforementioned labels. This interface enables dual supervision, as discussed in Section 2; labels are provided both for instances (citations) and features (words/n-grams). Both will ultimately be exploited by our learning algorithm, which is a variant of the Support Vector Machine (SVM) that incorporates the labeled terms during learning [8].

Figure 2 provides a schematic of the abstrackr system architecture. The numbered arrows in the figure indicate interactions and the general ‘flow’ of the system, which we now describe. (1) Researchers undertaking the review interact directly with the web application via the interface depicted in Figure 1. (2) The next citation to be screened is selected based on a priority table stored in the database. This table contains ranked lists of citations for each review in the system; these citations are ranked according to the AL function (e.g., uncertainty sampling) selected for the corresponding review. This is therefore our operationalization of AL. As previously discussed, there is a (sometimes substantial) computational cost associated with re-computing the AL score for each instance in the unlabeled pool, thus re-prioritizing the unlabeled citations can be slow. Any deployed AL system must address this issue, or else it risks being unresponsive, thereby undercutting the aim of making better use of expert time. Our strategy is to perform this reranking asynchronously: (3) abstrackr periodically calls on the machine learning library (also local to the server) to (4) re-sort the citations for the current review. This asynchronous re-ranking means that the reviewer doesn’t have to wait for the computer to decide which citation should be screened next; it is decided beforehand and immediately displayed to them.

Above, we mentioned the need to allocate labeling (screening) tasks in a way that makes the best use of the participating experts. In practice, abstrackr roughly follows the Multiple Expert Active Learning (MEAL) algorithm we have proposed elsewhere [11]. This method requires a ranking of the participants with respect to expertise; i.e., we need to know who of the participating screeners are likely to provide high-quality (correct) labels. We assume this expertise correlates with cost, that is, cheaper (less experienced) reviewers will tend to provide lower-quality labels compared to more expensive (experienced) reviewers. As a proxy for this information, we ask users how many systematic reviews they have previously participated in when they register for an account on abstrackr. When a less-experienced reviewer labels a citation with the ‘?’ button (see Figure 1), indicating that it is a borderline case (or that he or she is insuficiently confident as to whether it ought to be included or not), that citation is then re-assigned to a more experienced reviewer.

docs.title: 4. INITIAL USES
docs.text:
abstrackr remains very much a tool in development. As such, it has thus far functioned primarily as an annotation tool, i.e., a tool for citation screening. Indeed, abstrackr has been used to facilitate screening in over 50 systematic reviews already. We are still developing the machine learn ing techniques suitable for the case of citation screening, and we will eventually perform a large-scale validation of our methods in order to make a case for its reliability. We have therefore focused on implementing a flexible annotation tool that can accommodate the emerging machine learning techniques of: 1) active learning and 2) dual supervision. We have also operationalized our algorithm for allocating screening tasks with respect to the reviewers participating in a given review.

That said, abstrackr has been used in a few prospective cases already. However, because our large-scale validation remains to be performed, in these cases a trained assistant (not a physician) screened all of the citations that the algorithm excluded to double-check the classifier’s decisions. When uncertain about a particular citation, this assistant deferred to the project lead (a physician; i.e., a more experienced reviewer). In both cases, abstrackr did not produce any false negatives, that is, it never designated a relevant citation as being irrelevant.

More specifically, we performed prospective classification for two reviews: one concerning treatments for sleep apnea and the other investigating self-measured blood pressure. In the former, 14,368 citations were retrieved via the initial query and had to be screened; in the latter review (selfmeasured blood pressure), 9,550 citations were retrieved. Using the abstrackr system, reviewers screened these citations interactively, in order of their likelihood of being relevant (meeting the inclusion criteria), as predicted by the classification model.3 We continued this process until the model no longer classified any of the remaining unlabeled citations as relevant. At this point, the remaining abstracts were screened by the assistant.

In the case of sleep apnea, 8,358 of the 14,368 ( 60%) of the citations were screened before the model predicted that the remaining 6,010 were irrelevant. The assistant marked for review 126 of these, all of which were subsequently excluded. For self-measured blood pressure, the model predicted that the remaining citations were irrelevant once 5,632 (again about 60%) were screened. At this point, the remaining 3,918 were screened by the assistant, who flagged 48 of these as being possibly relevant. Again, all 48 were subsequently rejected by the project lead.

In summary: on both reviews for which the classification component of the abstrackr system has been deployed, it reduced workload (the number of citations that needed to be manually screened) by about 40% without wrongly excluding any relevant reviews, i.e., the sensitivity of the classifier was 100%. This was verified by an assistant doublechecking (screening) the citations that the system rejected. Once we’ve conducted our large-scale validation on many real-world systematic review datasets, this latter step of manually verifying the classifier’s decisions will no longer be required.

docs.title: 5. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
docs.text:
We have presented the abstrackr system for facilitating citation screening for systematic reviews. We view this as a case study in deploying a machine learning system for real-world use in a clinical research setting. Happily, abstrackr has been found useful as a collaborative annotation tool, independent of its machine learning components. By construction, abstrackr facilitates two emerging machine learning paradigms: active learning, in which the classification model is interactively trained by an expert (reviewer), and dual supervision, which allows the expert to impart domain knowledge to the model in the form of labeled terms.

The tool thus provides a mechanism for putting state-of-theart machine learning algorithms to use for the common and laborious clinical research task of citation screening.

abstrackr is completely open source and free to use for groups undertaking systematic reviews.4 The classification methods are not yet deployed to the public server (i.e., they are thus far only being used internally at our EPC), however, in the coming year we plan on integrating these more tightly with the web application.
