docs.title: 1. Motivation and significance
docs.text:
In recent years, the field of bibliometrics has gained considerable momentum in the research community [1]. Within the field of bibliometrics, scientific mapping is a method of visualizing and analyzing scientific research to identify the structure and dynamics of a field of study [2,3]. It uses the information in bibliometric data to determine the relatedness between publications based on for example shared authors, direct citation, bibliographic coupling, co-citation, or shared keywords.

The general process of scientific mapping includes the two main steps of (1) data-collection (and pre-processing) and (2) visualization and analysis [4,5]. The goal of PyblioNet is to support researchers when performing bibliometric analyses, scoping reviews or in their daily literature searches etc. by combining a Scopus data collection and pre-processing tool with a user-friendly and intuitive analysis and visualization tool. PyblioNet builds on the Python libraries Pybliometrics [6] and NetworkX [7], as well as the Javascript library vis.js [8], and can download publication data directly from the Scopus database via Scopus APIs and visualize/analyze the resulting network using a browser-based tool.

The three main advantages of PyblioNet in contrast to existing software capable of using Scopus data (e.g. Bibliometrix [9] Bibexcel [10], VOSviewer [11], Litstudy [12], CiteSpace [13], or SciMAT [14], see also [4,15] for detailed overviews of bibliometric software) are: (i) the ability to work with unique Scopus identifiers for authors and documents, which avoids the need for complex data cleaning and manual assignment [16,17], (ii) the possibility to collect further information on citing documents, e.g. to determine co-citation relationships, and (iii) the ability to include references and citing documents in the analysis and visualization, e.g. to scope for relevant literature.

More specifically, the main functions of PyblioNet include:

- literature searches based on Scopus advanced query strings

- calculation of publication networks based on shared authors, citation, bibliographic coupling, co-citation and shared keywords

- network manipulation and export of network data

- filtering of network nodes and links (by node type, publication date, degree centrality, network level or link weight)

- visualization and analysis tools (e.g. searching for specific nodes, resizing or recoloring nodes, force-directed or hierarchical layout)

Fig. 1. UML Activity diagram of the Python data collection too

- direct user interaction (e.g. manual repositioning of nodes, node popups with publication’s abstract, access to the full text of a publication via its DOI)

In order to use PyblioNet, users need access to the Scopus database and a valid Scopus API key which needs to be entered upon first usage. After that, the user can start entering Scopus advanced search query strings. After downloading publication data, an HTML file is generated that can be opened in a browser and contains all necessary data and visualization/analysis tools.

docs.title: 2.1. CLI data collection
docs.text:
PyblioNet consists of two main components. The first component is a Python-based data collection script which is built around the Pybliometrics library [6] to download publication data from the Scopus database via using Scopus Abstract Retrieval API and Search API (Fig. 1).

Users can use PyblioNet by executing a Python script, which requires the installation of the libraries such as Pybliometrics [6], NetworkX [7], etc. Alternatively, users can run the exe file, which includes all necessary libraries. For the first use, users need to enter a valid Scopus API key in order to access the database via Pybliometrics.1 After that, users can start by entering Scopus advanced search query strings.2 PyblioNet will display how many publications were found using the search query and ask the user if they want to continue. If so, the user can continue with a standard setting, or with an advanced mode where the user can decide on the following settings:

- Minimum citation count: exclude search results based on their cita tions. (default: 0).

- Use cached data if possible: download publication data even if it is data cached on your computer. (default: yes).

- Download information about citing papers: downloading informa tion on publications citing the search results is necessary for co citation analysis but takes additional time. (default: yes).

- Create extra nodes for references and citing papers: creating extra nodes for references and citing papers can result in huge networks that may be too large to visualize. If the user chooses “later”, PiblioNet will ask for a minimum occurrence of extra nodes for references and citing papers. (default: yes).

- Download abstracts: downloading abstracts for search results increases the size of the html file and takes additional time. (default: yes).

- Minimum weight for bibliographic coupling: include bibliographic coupling links between publications only if there are at least x shared references (reduces network size). (default: 1).

- Minimum weight for co-citation: include co-citation links between publications only if there are at least x shared citing publications (reduces network size). (default: 1).

- Minimum weight for shared keywords: include shared keyword link between publications only if there are at least x shared keywords (reduces network size). (default: 1).

- Create Gephi file: Creates an additional .gexf file of the network [18] which can be opened in Gephi. (default: no).

More specifically, PyblioNet first downloads information on the initial set of publications via Pybliometrics [6], which accesses the Scopus search API using Scopus advanced search query strings. In a second step, further information on references of the main search results are collected using the Abstract Retrieval API (“FULL” and “REF” view). Finally, citing publications are collected for each main search result via the Scopus Search API again. The publication data is then used to create network data using NetworkX [7] where each publication is represented as a node and relationships between nodes are visualized via links connecting nodes. PyblioNet covers five methods to determine network relationships:

- Shared authorship: nodes are connected if they share one or more authors (using Scopus author IDs).

- Citation: nodes are connected (via a directed link) if one cites the other (using Scopus EIDs).

- Bibliographic Coupling: nodes are connected if they share one or more references (using Scopus EIDs; only for Scopus main results).

- Co-citation: nodes are connected if they share one or more citing papers (using Scopus EIDs; only for Scopus main results).

- Shared keywords: nodes are connected if they share one or more keywords (using author keywords; only for Scopus main results).

Fig. 2. Example of a citation network of 173 main search results.

Finally, a HTML file is created that contains both the network data and the analysis and visualization tools.

docs.title: 2.2. Browser analysis and visualization tool
docs.text:
The second component is a HTML / JavaScript analysis and visualization tool building on the VisJs [8] package. The visualization and analysis tool is designed as a browser-based graphical interface that provides a user-friendly and intuitive way to navigate through complex publication data.

PyblioNet also allows for different filtering and visualization methods. First, users can choose to display only publication data from the main search results or also citing and cited publications. Further filtering of nodes can be done based on publication date, or the current degree centrality. Link filtering allows users to easily switch between the five network levels authorship, citation, bibliographic coupling, cocitation or shared keywords [5,19–21]. In the case of bibliographic coupling, co-citation and keyword relationships, links can additionally be filtered by their weight (representing the number of commonly cited or citing literature or keywords).

For visualization, users can enter search queries to highlight nodes where e.g. the search query “agent based and network” will highlight nodes that mention “agent based” and “network” in their keywords, title or abstract. Resizing nodes can be done based on nodes` current degree centrality (and in case of citation networks also based on their in-degree or out-degree) or number of citations. Recoloring of nodes can be done to identify cluster structures within large and dense networks using a Louvain community detection algorithm [21] as implemented by [22], or based on common journals (node colors are also used to identify clusters that are analyzed in more detail using the “Show information” button). The default visualization of nodes is based on a force-directed layout algorithm placing well-connected nodes in the center of the network and less well-connected nodes at the periphery [23]. Users can also choose to use a hierarchical layout where the y-coordinate of nodes in the canvas is based on the publication year, hereby positioning older publications at the top and newer ones at the bottom (in case of a citation network, for example, the hierarchical layout shows the cumulative nature of a research field). By changing the spring length users can define the distance between nodes and the nodes size defines the size of the nodes visualized.

Finally, the “Show information” button opens a new window showing the number of nodes and edges as well as the most frequent keywords and journals. If users have previously colored nodes (based on the Louvain algorithm or common journals), additional information for the communities is displayed. Additionally, users can delete selected nodes (for selecting multiple nodes, press and hold Ctrl), export the current set of nodes in a Gephi compatible format [18], or display additional navigation buttons.

PyblioNet also allows for direct user interaction such as repositioning nodes manually via drag-and-drop, hovering over nodes to get more information such as abstract, keywords etc. as well as highlighting nodes and their direct peers by clicking on a node e.g. to identify related literature. To quickly access the publication directly from the publisher, double-clicking on a node opens a new tab using the publication’s DOI or, if not available, opens google scholar with the publication’s title as a search query.

docs.title: 3.1. Literature search
docs.text:
In this section, we illustrate how users can use PyblioNet. A first use case of PyblioNet consists of performing literature searches in order to find, scan and evaluate relevant academic and scholarly articles or books to gather information on a specific topic. To illustrate this, we use the following example search query:

TITLE-ABS-KEY(("innovation diffusion" OR "diffusion of innovation") AND (agent-based OR multi-agent)) AND DOCTYPE(ar) aiming at finding relevant published articles within the field of innovation diffusion and applying the method of agent-based modelling. The search query results in 173 search results and in sum, these articles use 6342 references and are being cited by 1179 publications. After removing duplicates (e.g. two or more documents use the same reference) a network of 173 main documents, 4751 references and 967 citing papers is created (see also Fig. 2).

After opening the network in a browser, users can scan for relevant literature for example, by starting with well-connected or highly cited nodes. After identifying an interesting publication, the five different network levels allow for scanning nodes’ peers (so called snowballing [24]) to identify additional relevant publications. As PyblioNet downloads and visualizes also cited and citing literature, the snowballing, however, is not limited to the initial list of results but may contain further relevant publications not included in the initial search results.

citation network

Fig. 3. Example of articles published in SoftwareX.

docs.title: 3.2. Science mapping
docs.text:
A second use case addresses research questions within the broad field of bibliographic analysis and science mapping. For this we chose the example of published articles within the journal ‘SoftwareX’, obtained via the search query “ISSN(23527110)” which resulted in 984 articles using 24.422 references and 17.961 citing papers. Fig. 3 presents the resulting networks for the citation, co-citation and keyword analysis a well as bibliographic coupling.

The citation and co-citation analysis of articles published in SoftwareX show only sparsely connected networks where the majority of nodes remain isolated. This indicates that articles published in the journal neither recognize related articles nor are considered together by articles outside the journal. The bibliographic coupling and keyword analysis, however, indicate a strong common basis and a (perceived) thematical relatedness. A further analysis of the corresponding keywords of the communities in the bibliographic coupling network shows the following information for the two biggest communities.

Cluster: 1. with 177 nodes. docs.title: 4. Impact
docs.text:
PyblioNet complements the existing set of software designed to help researchers to perform bibliometric analysis and literature search. It offers a range of useful features that can change how researchers, educators, or institutions engage with bibliometric analysis, literature reviews, and knowledge exploration. By combining data collection and preprocessing with user-friendly visualization and analysis tools, PyblioNet provides a comprehensive platform for gaining deeper insights into the intricate web of scientific knowledge.

Fig. 4. citation network including information on referenced publications.

One of PyblioNet s standout features is its seamless integration with unique Scopus identifiers for authors and documents. This eliminates the need for time-consuming and error-prone manual data cleaning and assignment, resulting in more accurate and reliable bibliometric analyses and allows accessing and incorporating information on citing documents, and thus, co-citation relationships. The potential use cases are widespread and range from identifying gaps in existing research, developing research frameworks, identification of key authors and works, or synthesizing information.

Requirements for using PyblioNet is a valid Scopus API key as well as access to the Scopus API. The Python module exists also as standalone exe file and the visualization and analysis requires only a browser. A main disadvantage of PyblioNet against other software which uses data obtained directly from the Scopus homepage is speed and downloading all information for set of 100 main search results takes up to 15 minutes and more depending on the internet connections.

docs.title: 5. Conclusions
docs.text: In this paper, we presented PyblioNet, a software suite designed to support researchers in bibliometric analysis, scoping reviews, and daily literature searches. PyblioNet is a valuable addition to the bibliometrics field, providing researchers with an efficient and versatile tool for bibliometric analysis, literature searches, and science mapping. By streamlining data collection and offering extensive analysis and visualization capabilities, PyblioNet contributes to a deeper understanding of scholarly interactions and knowledge dissemination, fostering informed decision-making and advancing research in diverse domains.

docs.title: ReviQ: A systematic literature review workbench
<sub>Philipp</sub> <sub>Haindl</sub> iD
docs.text: University of Applied Sciences St. Pölten, Department of Computer Science & Security, St. Pölten, Austria

docs.title: A R T I C L E I N F O
docs.text: Keywords: Evidence-based software engineering PRISMA Reproducibility Research methodology tool Systematic literature review

docs.title: A B S T R A C T
docs.text: We present ReviQ, an open-source workbench for systematic literature reviews (SLRs) that runs locally in Docker and does not require cloud accounts. The tool implements all eight phases of the Kitchenham and Charters (2007) methodology: project setup, BibTeX import with cross-database deduplication, title/abstract screening, full-text eligibility, snowballing with saturation tracking, quality assessment, configurable data extraction, and results visualization, including PRISMA 2020 flow diagrams. Reviewer agreement is quantified through Cohen’s � with asymptotic confidence intervals and PABAK, which is computed directly from the stored decisions. The complete project state—decisions, conflict resolutions, QA scores, extraction records, taxonomies, and source BibTeX files— can be exported as a versioned replication package and re-imported into another ReviQ instance, enabling third parties to audit or continue a review. We validated ReviQ by conducting a complete SLR on a software engineering topic across five databases, four snowballing iterations, 519 retrieved and 356 screened papers, involving two reviewers and resulting in 40 included studies. ReviQ is released under the GPL v3 license

docs.title: 1 . Motivation and significance
docs.text:
The systematic literature review (SLR), as outlined by Kitchenham and Charters [1] within the context of evidence-based software engineering [2], comprises three main phases. Planning establishes the research questions, the search strategy across the chosen databases, and the inclusion/exclusion criteria. Conduct covers the execution of the database searches and the processing of candidates through screening by at least two independent reviewers, full-text eligibility assessment, optional citation snowballing [3], quality assessment, and structured data extraction. Reporting synthesises the extracted data and documents the entire process—most prominently via a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 [4,5] flow diagram—so that the review can be audited and replicated. Each phase generates artefacts—decision logs, conflict records, agreement statistics, and PRISMA counts among them—which must be internally consistent and accessible for replication.

Table 2 Feature comparison of SLR tools. ∙ = supported, ◦ = partial, – = not supported.

FeatureRayyanStArtParsifalCovidenceReviQOpen source•••-•Runs locally-•--•BibTeX deduplication•○•••Dual-reviewer screening•○○••Conflict resolution UI○--••Cohen's κ / PABAK----•Snowballing tracking-•--•Quality assessment-••○•Configurable extraction-○○••PRISMA 2020 diagram---••Replication-package export----•

Since 2007, SLRs have become a widely adopted research methodology in the field of software engineering [6]. Subsequent work has highlighted both their increasing utilization and the recurring methodological challenges associated with them [7,8]. A primary concern in this context is the issue of tooling. When we conducted an SLR on a JVM-related topic, we initially documented decisions using a shared spreadsheet. It soon became evident that this approach was inadequate—parallel edits resulted in merge conflicts, the � computation required re-derivation with each decision change, and the PRISMA numbers in the manuscript frequently diverged from the actual counts until discrepancies were identified. This experience, which appears to be common among software engineering researchers [9,10], prompted the development of ReviQ.

Numerous tools have been developed to address various aspects of this issue. Marshall et al. [11] ofer a systematic feature analysis of existing SLR tools, while Al-Zubidy et al. [12] identify a prioritized set of value-added requirements for SLR tooling infrastructure. Rayyan [13] has emerged as the most widely adopted screening tool, featuring an intuitive web interface with semi-automated duplicate detection and label-based filtering; however, it is cloud-hosted and does not support phases beyond screening. StArt [14] encompasses the entire systematic reviewing process, including quality assessment (QA), and has recently incorporated snowballing support; nonetheless, it does not compute inter-rater agreement nor generate PRISMA 2020 diagrams. Parsifal1 provides a web-based, protocol-driven workflow with quality assessment but lacks snowballing, � calculation, and any form of replicationpackage export. Covidence2 is extensively utilized in the health sciences and ofers a refined dual-reviewer workflow with PRISMA output, yet it is a commercial cloud product with a free tier limited to a single review. Table 2 presents a comparison of features across these tools.

We developed ReviQ to address the existing gaps: a single, locallydeployable application that encompasses all phases of the Kitchenham and Charters methodology, calculates � with confidence intervals, generates PRISMA 2020 diagrams from live data, and consolidates the entire project state into a portable replication package. The tool operates within Docker, stores all data in a local SQLite database, and does not connect to any external servers.

Fig. 1. Two-container architecture of ReviQ. Container 1 serves the React frontend via Nginx; Container 2 runs the FastAPI backend with a persisted SQLite database. Both run on the researcher’s machine.

The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 describes the architecture of ReviQ and its eight functional phases. Section 3 il lustrates ReviQ on a real validation SLR involving five databases, four snowballing iterations, and two independent reviewers. Section 4 discusses the tool’s research and educational impact, its positioning against related tools, and current limitations. Section 5 concludes.

docs.title: 2.1 . Software architecture
docs.text:
ReviQ is a Docker [15] application comprising two containers, as illustrated in Fig. 1. The first container operates Nginx, which serves the React single-page application and reverse-proxies /api/* requests to the second container, a FastAPI [16] service implemented in Python 3.12. All state data is maintained within a SQLite database on a designated Docker volume (reviq-db-data), ensuring data persistence across container rebuilds. Initiating the application merely requires executing docker compose up --build; there is no necessity for configuring accounts, application programming interface (API) keys, or external databases.

The backend comprises ten route modules—one per SLR phase plus cross-cutting concerns like kappa, export, and report—and two service modules (bibtex_service for parsing and deduplication, kappa_service for agreement statistics). The database schema is structured with 16 SQLModel [17] tables that align with the SLR process, encompassing projects, reviewers, inclusion/exclusion/QA criteria, papers, reviewer decisions, final decisions, conflict logs, QA scores, extraction fields and records, snowballing iterations, taxonomy entries, database search strings, and paper–database links. The frontend operates exclusively through the REST API, with React Query managing all data retrieval and cache invalidation, thereby ensuring that the user interface is promptly updated upon the recording of a decision.

docs.title: 2.2 . Software functionalities
docs.text:
ReviQ realises the SLR methodology as eight sequential phases that map onto the three main phases introduced in Section 1: Phase 1 (project setup) corresponds to Planning; Phases 2–7 (import, screening, eligibility, snowballing, quality assessment, and data extraction) constitute Conduct; and Phase 8 (results and PRISMA visualisation) constitutes Reporting. Fig. 2 illustrates the eight-phase ReviQ workflow, highlighting which phases are dual-reviewer activities, the iterative snowballing loop, and the final output phase. The sidebar of the application organizes these phases in the same sequential order. At the top of each phase page, a statistics bar displays real-time counts (retrieved, unique, duplicates, included, excluded, undecided), providing the reviewer with a continuous sense of progress.

Fig. 2. Eight-phase SLR workflow following Kitchenham and Charters [1]. The dashed arrow indicates that snowballing [3] feeds new candidates back into screening.

Phase 1—Setup. The researcher initiates a project by establishing a title, description, and the name of the lead researcher, and registers up to five reviewers. Inclusion and exclusion criteria are delineated for each phase (screening or full-text), with each criterion assigned a label (e.g., E3) and a concise, human-readable name that subsequently appears in the exclusion breakdown of the PRISMA diagram. Quality assessment criteria are configured with a maximum score of either 0.5 or 1.0. Taxonomy categories (e.g., “Research Type” with values such as “Evaluation Research”, “Solution Proposal”, etc.) and custom extraction fields (free text, number, boolean, dropdown) are also defined at this stage. Finally, for each database, the researcher documents the search string, filter settings, search date, and result count—this metadata is directly incorporated into the generated protocol report.

Phase 2—Import. BibTeX files are uploaded for each database from a directory on the host machine. ReviQ processes these files using bibtexparser [18] and performs deduplication across databases in two stages: initially based on the normalized Digital Object Identifier (DOI; converted to lowercase and stripped of whitespace), followed by a composite key of normalized title and normalized venue for entries lacking a DOI. The normalization process removes punctuation and collapses whitespace, thereby addressing minor formatting discrepancies between databases (e.g., “Proc. ICSE” versus “Proceedings of ICSE”). Each identified duplicate is logged with the citekey of the retained original; reviewers have the option to examine this log and override individual decisions if the heuristic proves incorrect. Language detection via langid flags non-English abstracts, facilitating the eficient application of exclusion criterion E3. A many-to-many link table (PaperDatabaseLink) records which databases identified each paper, enabling the calculation of per-database precision and recall in Phase 7.

Phase 3—Screening. Each reviewer independently categorizes every paper as Include (I), Exclude (E), or Uncertain (U), with the option to select the governing criterion (e.g., E2—insuficient focus) and provide a free-text rationale. Papers are presented individually, displaying their title, authors, year, venue, abstract, and source database; a filter bar at the top facilitates narrowing the list to undecided, included, excluded, or uncertain items. Decisions are recorded per reviewer in the ReviewerDecision table. The backend system compares decisions between the two primary reviewers and identifies disagreements as conflicts. These conflicts are displayed in a dedicated conflict tab (Fig. 4), where each conflict shows the paper title, both reviewers’ decisions with their rationales side by side, and controls to resolve the conflict through discussion or arbitration. The resolution method and an optional note are documented in the ConflictLog table. Decisions can be exported as a JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) file, allowing co-reviewers working on separate machines to exchange them via email or shared drives and import them back; the source_file field on each imported decision preserves provenance.

Fig. 3 presents the screening view of Phase 3, with the paper list, per-paper decision badges, the total/undecided/included/excluded/uncertain counters, and the filter bar used to narrow the list during the review. Fig. 4 illustrates the conflict resolution view, displaying both reviewers’ decisions for a disputed paper alongside their rationales and the controls used to record the resolution.

Phase 4—Eligibility. The same decision-making process is applicable to the full-text assessment, utilizing the inclusion and exclusion criteria established in Phase 1. Articles may include a full-text URL for expedited access or be marked as inaccessible if the full text cannot be obtained.

Phase 5—Snowballing. Forward and backward citation chasing is conducted in accordance with Wohlin [3]. Each iteration is represented as a distinct entity within the database. The researcher imports a new BibTeX batch labeled snowballing:N (where � denotes the iteration number), which subsequently undergoes the standard screening and eligibility process. The iteration overview (Fig. 5) illustrates, for each iteration, the number of candidates retrieved, decided, included after screening, excluded, and those still undecided, along with a saturation indicator. When an iteration results in zero new inclusions, the researcher may designate it as saturated, indicating that the snowballing process has reached convergence.

Phase 6—Quality assessment. In the evaluation process, included papers are assessed according to the QA criteria established in Phase 1. Each criterion is assigned a score of 0, 0.5, or 1 by individual reviewers. These scores are then normalized to a percentage and categorized as high (≥ 75% by default), medium (≥ 50%), or low, with both thresholds being adjustable for each project. A summary view provides an overview of the score distribution across all papers; Fig. 6 shows this distribution for the validation SLR.

Phase 7—Data extraction. The extraction schema delineated in Phase 1 accommodates four distinct field types: free text, numerical, boolean, and dropdown with project-specific option lists. Taxonomy categories furnish an additional structured classification layer. A card view enumerates all papers, accompanied by a progress badge indicating the number of fields completed; a table view ofers a spreadsheet-style overview of all extraction records, which can be exported as comma-separated values (CSV). Fig. 7 illustrates the Research Type and Contribution Type taxonomy distributions for the validation SLR.

Phase 8—Results. The output is organized into three tabs. The PRISMA Flow tab presents a PRISMA 2020 [4] diagram as an inline SVG, featuring two parallel streams (database search and snowballing) and exclusion breakdowns per criterion. This diagram is available for download in both colour and greyscale variants suitable for publication. The Charts tab provides visualisations along four reporting dimensions and is deliberately not limited to selection metrics. For selection, it shows per-database

Fig. 3. Screening (Phase 3) showing a paper list with decision badges and a filter bar.

Fig. 4. Conflict resolution view showing both reviewers’ decisions and resolution rationale.

precision, recall, and F1 scores together with a publication-year histogram and a venue distribution. For agreement, it shows Cohen’s � and PABAK with 95% confidence intervals per review phase. For quality, it shows the QA score distribution against the low/medium/high thresh olds. For synthesis, it shows a taxonomy-category distribution across the contribution- and research-type taxonomies and an aggregation of any user-defined extraction field. All charts are rendered as scalable vector graphics (SVG) and can be downloaded individually from the application, making them directly suitable for inclusion in publications without further processing. The same charts are also embedded in the supplementary PDF protocol report. The Export tab ofers four download options: a replication package (.zip) containing the complete project state and all BibTeX files, a PDF protocol report generated via fpdf2, a CSV extraction dataset, and BibTeX files categorized by inclusion status (included after screening, included after full-text, excluded).

Inter-rater agreement. ReviQ calculates Cohen’s � [19,20] using a 3 × 3 confusion matrix comprising the categories Include, Exclude, and

Fig. 5. Snowballing (Phase 5) with four forward iterations. Iteration 4 included zero new papers, confirming saturation.

Fig. 6. Quality score distribution (Phase 6, Charts tab) for the validation SLR: 40 papers assessed; low/medium/high thresholds at 50% and 75%; mean 80.5%, median 88.9%. The chart is available for download as an SVG.

Uncertain. The category Uncertain is maintained as a separate entity rather than being merged with Include or Exclude, as reviewers intentionally use it to identify borderline cases requiring further discussion. Let � represent the number of papers for which both reviewers have rendered a decision. The observed agreement is given by $\begin{array} { r } { P _ { o } = \frac { 1 } { n } \sum _ { c } n _ { c c } , } \end{array}$ while the expected agreement is $\begin{array} { r } { P _ { e } = \sum _ { c } ( R _ { c } / n ) ( C _ { c } / n ) . } \end{array}$ where $R _ { c }$ and $C _ { c }$ denote the row and column marginals, respectively. Consequently, $\kappa = ( P _ { o } - P _ { e } ) / ( 1 - P _ { e } )$ . The 95% confidence interval is derived using the asymptotic standard error as described by Fleiss [21]. Given that SLR screening data are typically imbalanced, with the majority of papers being excluded, ReviQ also provides PABAK [22] $( = 2 P _ { o } - 1 )$ , which accounts for prevalence and bias. Both metrics are interpreted according to the Landis and Koch [23] scale, which ranges from “poor” to “almost perfect” agreement. For projects involving more than two reviewers, all pairwise � values can be computed in a single request via the /kappa/all-pairs endpoint. Fig. 8 illustrates the agreement dashboard as presented in the application.

Reproducibility and sharing. ReviQ supports two complementary modes of sharing the review. The first is in-progress decision exchange: since reviewers work on separate machines without a shared server, each dualreviewer phase (Phase 3 Screening and Phase 4 Eligibility) provides an Export Decisions button that writes the current reviewer’s decisions to a JSON file, and an Import Decisions button that reads a co-reviewer’s JSON file into the local database. Importing a co-reviewer’s decisions immediately triggers automatic conflict detection—any paper on which the two reviewers disagree appears in the conflict tab without any manual comparison step. Both buttons invoke the operating system’s standard file-selection dialog; the JSON file itself can be transmitted via any channel (email, shared drive, USB stick). The source_file field on each imported decision records its provenance, so the origin of every decision is traceable.

The second mode is full-project replication: the Export tab in Phase 8 ofers a Replication Package download—a versioned ZIP archive containing the complete project state: decisions, conflict resolutions, QA

Fig. 7. Research Type (left) and Contribution Type (right) taxonomy distributions (Phase 7/8, Charts tab) for the validation SLR: 40 papers across 4 categories each. Charts are available for download as SVG

Fig. 8. Agreement dashboard: � = 0.509 (95% CI [0.331, 0.687]), PABAK = 0.486 Landis & Koch: “Moderate agreement”.

scores, extraction records, taxonomies, and all BibTeX source files. Any researcher can import this archive into a local ReviQ instance via the + Import Package action on the Overview page, which reproduces the review verbatim. This makes the package suitable for archival deposit alongside a publication, for transferring work between team members, or for providing a verifiable replication artefact to reviewers of the SLR paper itself. The same Export tab generates a PDF protocol report via fpdf2, covering the research protocol, per-database search strings and result counts, the PRISMA diagram, screening and eligibility statistics with � and PABAK, QA results, the extraction dataset, and a bibliography of all included papers.

docs.title: 3 . Illustrative example
docs.text:
We employed ReviQ to perform an SLR on the usage patterns of a Java runtime interface. The review was conducted by two reviewers and encompassed five databases searched in February 2026: Scopus (217), IEEE Xplore (162), ACM DL (172), SpringerLink (56), and DBLP (1), totalling 608 hits. After BibTeX export and import, 495 records were available for deduplication; ReviQ identified and removed 139 duplicates via DOI and normalized title/venue matching, leaving 356 unique papers.

Six inclusion criteria were defined to capture papers describing the technology under review, discussing its practical applications, addressing challenges, or utilizing documented frameworks built upon it. Eleven exclusion criteria covered duplicates, insuficient focus, non-English publications, theses, non-peer-reviewed work, and of-topic domains.

docs.title: 3.1 . Database stream
docs.text: Of the 356 screened papers, 326 were excluded at the title/abstract screening, leaving 30 papers for full-text assessment. Of these, 6 were excluded at the full-text stage, yielding 24 included studies from the database search.

docs.title: 3.2 . Snowballing stream
docs.text:
Four forward citation iterations were conducted following Wohlin [3]. Iterations 1 through 3 retrieved 9, 8, and 4 candidates, of which 7, 6, and 3 were included respectively. Iteration 4 retrieved 3 candidates but included none, confirming saturation. Of the 24 candidates retrieved in total, 8 were excluded during screening; the remaining 16 proceeded to full-text assessment, all of which were included, yielding 16 additional studies. The two streams together yielded a final corpus of 40 studies. Fig. 9 presents the PRISMA 2020 diagram generated by ReviQ from the live project data.

Cohen’s � for screening was 0.509 (95% CI [0.331, 0.687]; PABAK = 0.486), indicating moderate agreement per Landis and Koch [23]. At full-text eligibility, both reviewers agreed on every paper (� = 1.0).

Fig. 9. PRISMA 2020 diagram generated by ReviQ for the validation SLR. Left: database search (� = 495 records from five databases, 24 included). Right: snowballing ( candidates from four iterations, 16 included). Exclusion boxes list per-criterion counts. The diagram is available for download in both colour and greyscale (For interpretation of the references to colour in this figure legend, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.)

Nineteen screening conflicts were resolved by discussion; none required third-party arbitration.

Quality assessment used nine binary criteria covering research objective clarity, technical depth, empirical evaluation, threats to validity, replication support, related work comparison, contribution clarity, evaluation subject appropriateness, and performance measurement. The mean score was 80.6%, with 28 high-, 9 medium-, and 3 low-quality studies.

docs.title: 4 . Impact
docs.text:
From a research standpoint, ReviQ significantly reduces the barriers to conducting methodologically rigorous systematic literature reviews. The integrated � computation eliminates a step that researchers frequently defer to a separate spreadsheet, often resulting in inconsistent calculations—sometimes applied to an incorrect subset of papers, sometimes using a 2×2 matrix when a 3×3 matrix would be more appropriate, and occasionally omitted altogether. The live updates of � and PABAK as decisions are recorded facilitate continuous monitoring of agreement throughout the review process, rather than solely at its conclusion.

The generation of the PRISMA diagram from the same database that stores the decisions ensures that the numbers in the diagram are consistent with the decision log [24]. This provides stronger assurance than a manually drawn figure, as our pre-ReviQ experience demonstrated that altering a single screening decision could inadvertently invalidate the PRISMA counts in the manuscript, with discrepancies only becoming apparent during a meticulous final review—if at all.

The replication-package export consolidates the entire project state into a versioned ZIP archive, thereby supporting the reproducibility requirements that several software engineering venues have begun to mandate. When published alongside an SLR, this package enables other researchers to verify reported counts against actual decisions, reuse the extraction data for meta-analyses, or extend the review with additional snowballing iterations.

The decision to run all processes locally was intentional. Researchers at institutions with restrictive data policies—or those handling embargoed submissions—may be prohibited from uploading paper metadata to a third-party cloud service. ReviQ does not contact any external server. The Docker-based deployment ensures consistent behavior across Linux, macOS, and Windows without necessitating the manual installation of Python, Node.js, or any other runtime.

Beyond its primary research application, ReviQ can also serve as an educational tool. By enforcing the Kitchenham and Charters phase structure and making each step explicit—criteria definition before screening, dual-reviewer decisions before conflict resolution, and QA scoring before extraction—it provides students with a concrete, interactive walkthrough of the SLR methodology.

docs.title: Discussion and comparison with related tools
docs.text:
No single feature sets ReviQ apart from existing tools; the diferentiator is their combination. Among the surveyed tools (Section 1, Table 2), Rayyan [13] ofers a polished cloud screening experience with label-based filtering but is confined to the screening phase, does not compute inter-rater agreement, and does not produce PRISMA diagrams. Covidence ofers a refined dual-reviewer workflow with PRISMA output, but is a commercial cloud product and—in the free tier—is limited to a single review per researcher. Among free, open-source tools, StArt [14] covers the broadest set of phases and has recently added snowballing, but does not compute � or PABAK, does not produce PRISMA 2020 diagrams, and ofers no equivalent to a singlefile replication-package export. Parsifal supports a protocol-driven workflow with quality assessment but lacks snowballing, agreement statistics, and replication-package export. ReviQ therefore combines local-only deployment, end-to-end phase coverage, integrated � and PABAK with confidence intervals, PRISMA 2020 generation from live data, and a single-file replication-package export—each available elsewhere in isolation but, to our knowledge, not jointly in a free and open-source tool.

The validation SLR was a small but realistic exercise of these capabilities. Screening agreement settled at the lower end of the Landis–Koch “moderate” band $( \kappa ~ = ~ 0 . 5 0 9 ) ;$ had this been computed only at the review’s end, it would have been too late to inform reviewer calibration. Because ReviQ surfaced � as decisions were recorded, the value prompted a mid-review conversation about how strictly to apply criterion E2 (insuficient focus); we found this more informative than a single end-of-review snapshot. The 19 screening conflicts were all resolved by discussion rather than third-party arbitration, suggesting that screening disagreements are typically matters of interpretation rather than systematic error. Of the four snowballing iterations, only iterations 1–3 contributed new included papers; iteration 4 yielded zero inclusions and was marked as saturated, which made the decision to stop a quantitative rather than an intuitive one. The PRISMA diagram, regenerated from live data at submission time, agreed with the manually verified counts—a check our pre-ReviQ experience suggests would otherwise have required a separate manual reconciliation pass.

Limitations. Several limitations remain. The asynchronous collaboration model, which relies on JSON export/import, works well for teams of two or three but does not scale for larger groups; a Git-based or sharedfilesystem sync layer is a planned enhancement. Currently, only BibTeX is supported as an import format; incorporating RIS and CSV import capabilities would enhance compatibility with databases that default to alternative formats. ReviQ does not yet provide AI-assisted screening, although the decision data stored within ReviQ, including paper metadata, reviewer labels, and rationales, could serve as training data for active-learning rankers. The PRISMA diagram presently implements only the two-stream layout as prescribed by the PRISMA 2020 statement (databases + other methods); reviews with more complex identification paths would require manual adjustments to the generated SVG. Lastly, ReviQ does not currently enforce blinding between reviewers—both reviewers can view each other’s names, although they cannot access each other’s decisions until they are exchanged.

docs.title: 5 . Conclusions
docs.text:
We have introduced ReviQ, an open-source SLR workbench that comprehensively addresses all eight phases of the Kitchenham and Charters methodology within a locally-deployed web application. The primary contributions of ReviQ, which extend beyond the capabilities of existing tools, include: (i) integrated computation of Cohen’s � and PABAK with confidence intervals, updated in real-time as decisions are made; (ii) automatic generation of PRISMA 2020 diagrams with exclusion counts per criterion, rendered as publication-ready SVGs; and (iii) a versioned replication-package export that consolidates all project data for archival purposes or transfer.

We validated the tool through application to a real SLR in the software engineering domain. This review involved two reviewers, five databases, 519 retrieved records, four snowballing iterations, and 40 included studies. The moderate screening agreement $( \kappa = 0 . 5 0 9 )$ and the resolution of 19 conflicts via the built-in user interface demonstrate the tool’s capability to manage typical levels of disagreement encountered in practice. The PRISMA diagram and a 22-page protocol report were generated directly from the stored data, afirming that ReviQ can facilitate a review from initial setup to publication-ready outputs without the need for external tools.

Future developments will focus on enabling real-time collaboration between reviewer instances, supporting RIS/CSV import, incorporating AI-assisted pre-screening, and implementing reviewer blinding.

docs.title: ScopusLit: An end-to-end Web-based tool for bibliometric analysis
docs.text:
Orlando Arroyo

Universidad Industrial de Santander, Bucaramanga, Santander, Colombia

docs.title: A R T I C L E I N F O
docs.text: Keywords: Bibliometric analysis Scopus Systematic literature review Topic modeling

docs.title: A B S T R A C T
docs.text: Bibliometric analysis supports systematic literature reviews, but it often requires disconnected tools for search, data storage, analysis, visualization, and export. This paper presents ScopusLit, an open-source, browser-based application for analyzing scientific literature indexed in Scopus through an integrated, zero-code workflow. Developed in Python with Streamlit and pybliometrics, ScopusLit executes Scopus Advanced Search queries through the API, retrieves abstracts, stores reproducible JSON datasets, and provides bibliometric, network, and abstract-level text analyses. Its functionality is demonstrated using a search query that retrieved 1036 records in 52 s and downloaded abstracts with 100% success in 678 s. The example illustrates temporal, geographic, keyword, co-occurrence, TF-IDF, and topic-modeling outputs, including network generation and NMF topic modeling. By combining Scopus-based retrieval, analysis, consolidation, and publication-ready export in a single web interface, ScopusLit reduces manual transfers between tools and supports reproducible bibliometric workflows for review-oriented research.

docs.title: 1. Motivation and significance
docs.text:
Bibliometric analysis is a cornerstone of systematic literature reviews, research trend identification, and science mapping [1]. Researchers frequently rely on the Scopus database, one of the largest curated abstract and citation databases of peer-reviewed literature, encompassing over 27,000 titles from >7000 publishers [2]. However, conducting rigorous bibliometric studies typically requires combining multiple disconnected tools: Scopus’s web interface for search, spreadsheet software for data cleaning, specialized bibliometric software for analysis, and graphic design tools for producing publication-quality figures.

While several established tools facilitate these analyses, they often present distinct limitations. For instance, VOSviewer [3] excels in the network visualization of co-authorship, co-citation, and keyword co-occurrence, yet it lacks text analysis capabilities and requires manual data importation. Similarly, Bibliometrix [4] offers comprehensive bibliometric indicators but demands proficiency in R programming. Tools like CiteSpace [5] and Publish or Perish [6] also exhibit constraints, either by relying on manual file transfers or offering limited visualization and text analysis capabilities. Consequently, none of these alternatives provides an integrated, zero-code workflow that spans from Scopus query execution to abstract-level text analysis. Conversely, programmatic solutions such as the pybliometrics Python library [7] offer robust API access but requires coding expertise, limiting accessibility for non-programmers.

To bridge this gap, this paper introduces ScopusLit, a web-based application designed for the comprehensive bibliometric analysis of Scopus-indexed literature. Developed in Python using the Streamlit web framework [8] and the pybliometrics API client [7], ScopusLit delivers an end-to-end workflow. The tool executes Advanced Search queries, persists results locally, generates over 20 types of bibliometric visualizations, performs natural language processing on abstracts, and exports publication-ready datasets and figures. It is specifically designed to support researchers, graduate students, and authors who require a streamlined process for producing review articles and comparing multiple search strategies.

ScopusLit has three distinctive features. First, it consolidates search execution, full abstract retrieval, and analysis into a single environment, eliminating manual file transfers. Second, it natively integrates advanced text analytics—specifically TF-IDF extraction and topic modeling (NMF/LDA) on abstracts. Third, its consolidation feature enables union and comparison modes via Venn overlap analysis, directly supporting the multi-query workflows essential to the PRISMA systematic review methodology [9].

docs.title: 2.1. Software architecture
docs.text:
ScopusLit is implemented as a single Python file (app.py) organized into 10 sections. The application follows a functional programming paradigm with grouped utility functions comprising 74 functions in total. While this design favors portability and ease of inspection, the functional nature is friendly to modularization to improve maintainability and scalability. Running the main script starts a local Streamlit web server accessible from any browser.

The application follows a three-layer separation. The data layer (Sections 2–4 of the source code) handles all interactions with external systems, including Scopus API communication via pybliometrics for searches and abstract retrieval, and local file system operations for JSON persistence. All API calls are wrapped in retry logic to respect Scopus rate limits. The analysis layer (Section 5-6 of the source code) contains pure computation functions that take pandas DataFrames or abstract dictionaries as input and return processed data structures. These functions have no side effects and no dependency on Streamlit, making them independently testable. Section 5 covers bibliometric computations (publication counts, author rankings, citation statistics, and cooccurrence network analysis), while Section 6 covers natural language processing (TF-IDF vectorization, topic modeling, word cloud generation). The presentation layer (Sections 7–9 of the source code) handles all visualization using Plotly [10] and matplotlib [11], data export via openpyxl [12] and pandas, and user interface rendering through Streamlit components, session state, and page routing.

ScopusLit uses Streamlit’s session state mechanism to persist appli cation state across user interactions, since Streamlit re-executes the entire script on every widget interaction. Eleven state variables manage the currently loaded search, cached DataFrames, h-index data, topic modeling results, and navigation state. Loading a search populates the search data and its derived DataFrame; loading a consolidation populates the merged DataFrame and combined abstracts. Each search is stored as a self-contained JSON file with a UUID-based filename in a local data directory, capturing the query string, execution date, complete result set, and any downloaded abstracts.

docs.title: 2.2. Software functionalities
docs.text:
ScopusLit implements 20 features organized into five functional categories: search and storage, bibliometric analysis, abstract text analysis, search consolidation, and export.

• Search and Storage. Users initiate the workflow Fig. 1 by entering a Scopus Advanced Search query. To conserve API quotas, ScopusLit features a "Result Estimation" function that retrieves the expected document count before initiating a full download. Once executed, the search results—including all metadata—are saved automatically. Users can subsequently trigger the abstract download module, which retrieves full abstract texts incrementally, saving progress every 25 documents to prevent data loss during long retrieval processes or network interruptions.

• Bibliometric Analysis. Upon loading a saved search, a tabbed interface provides comprehensive, interactive visualizations of the dataset. Key analyses include:

○ Timeline and Sources: A dual-axis chart displays publications per year alongside cumulative growth, while a horizontal bar chart identifies the top 15 publishing journals. ScopusLit citation analysis is implemented through the Scopus citedby_count field. The software computes total citations, mean citations, median citations, and maximum citations for the retrieved corpus. It also identifies the top 20 most cited documents, generates a citation distribution histogram, and plots average citations by publication year. The software groups publications by year, calculates cumulative publication counts, identifies the peak publication year, and visualizes annual production trends.

○ Geography and Authorship: Geographic distribution is mapped using an interactive choropleth world map, alongside top contributing countries and affiliations. The author tab highlights top contributors and features an on-demand "Fetch h-index" tool that queries the AuthorRetrieval API. Co-authorship and collaboration patterns are addressed through both tabular and networkbased analyses. The software extracts author names from Scopus metadata, counts the most productive authors, identifies frequent

docs.title: ScopusLit Software Workflow
docs.text:
Fig. 1. ScopusLit workflow and features.

co-author pairs, and visualizes the distribution of authors per article. In addition, it builds co-occurrence networks using networkx, including author co-authorship networks, keyword cooccurrence networks, and country collaboration networks. These networks include adjustable thresholds, node limits, selectable layouts, community detection, and summary metrics such as number of nodes, edges, communities, density, and average degree. trend analysis is addressed through temporal and thematic evolution tools.

○ Keywords and Citations: Keyword frequencies are visualized through bar charts and word clouds. Citation analysis provides distribution histograms, summary metrics, and temporal citation trends. ScopusLit tracks keyword evolution over time by crosstabulating the most frequent author keywords by publication year and displaying them as a heatmap.

• Abstract Text Analysis. When abstracts are successfully retrieved, ScopusLit unlocks an advanced natural language processing (NLP) pipeline.

The text-analysis workflow has three components. First, the abstract word cloud concatenates all non-empty abstracts and removes a combined stopword list composed of the default wordcloud English stop words, an added Spanish stopword list, and additional domain-generic terms such as “abstract,” “study,” “results,” “method,” “research,” “analysis,” “data,” “model,” “et,” and “al.”

Second, the TF-IDF module uses scikit-learn’s TfidfVectorizer [13]. The default parameters are: max_features=1000, stop_words="english", max_df=0.85, min_df=2, and ngram_range=(1, 2). Thus, the system considers unigrams and bigrams, excludes very common terms appearing in >85% of abstracts, excludes terms appearing in fewer than two abstracts, and returns the top 30 terms ranked by average TF-IDF score across the corpus. At least three non-empty abstracts are required. Third, topic modeling is performed on TF-IDF vectors using either Non-negative Matrix Factorization or Latent Dirichlet Allocation, selected by the user in the interface. The default method is NMF, and the default number of topics is five. Users can choose between 3 and 10 topics through a slider. The topic model uses max_features=2000, stop_words="english", max_df=0.85, and min_df=2. For NMF, the software uses n_components=n_topics, random_state=42, and max_iter=300; for LDA, it uses n_components=n_topics, random_- state=42, and max_iter=20. The model requires at least max(5, n_topics) non-empty abstracts. ScopusLit provides an exploratory interface in which the user specifies the desired granularity. A lower number of topics gives broader thematic groupings, whereas a higher number gives more specific but potentially more fragmented themes. Importantly, the TF-IDF is implemented in the compute_tfidf_terms(); NMF/LDA topic modeling is implemented in compute_topic_model() .

• Search Consolidation. To support complex systematic reviews that require the synthesis of multiple search strings, ScopusLit includes a powerful consolidation module. Researchers can select multiple saved searches and merge them in one of two modes:

○ Union mode: Concatenates datasets and automatically dedupli cates entries based on the Scopus unique identifier (EID), applying the full Phase 2 and 3 analytical pipeline to the merged corpus.

○ Comparison Mode: Generates comparative visualizations, including overlaid publication timelines, grouped keyword bar charts, and a document overlap analysis utilizing tabular statistics and Venn diagrams based on Matplotlib [14,15] (for up to three searches) to illustrate the precise intersection of different research queries.

• Export Capabilities. The platform ensures comprehensive data portability. Full results and analytical summaries can be exported as CSV files or multi-sheet Excel workbooks. Concurrently, all charts—which adhere to a cohesive visual specification utilizing the color-blind friendly Set2 palette—can be exported as publicationready 300 DPI PNG files via the Kaleido rendering engine [16] and Matplotlib.

User navigation is seamlessly routed through a four-page structure (New Search, Saved Searches, Analysis, Consolidation), supported by a persistent sidebar for rapid access to saved datasets.

docs.title: 3. Illustrative example
docs.text:
This example demonstrates and profiles the performance of ScopusLit using the search equation: TITLE-ABS-KEY(("learning analytics" OR "academic analytics" OR "educational data mining") AND ("at-risk student*" OR "student risk" OR "academic risk" OR "early warning" OR "early alert" OR "dropout prediction" OR "student performance prediction" OR "course failure" OR "academic failure") AND ("predictive model*" OR "risk model*" OR "machine learning" OR "classification" OR "prediction" OR "analytics dashboard*" OR "early warning system*")). The goal of this search was a broad search on analytics applications to quantify student risk, especially in learning analytics / educational data mining. A companion video demonstrating the application functionality with another search equation is also available at the link referenced in the Code Metadata Table. After inserting the equation, the results estimation was 1036 documents, whose title information was recovered in 52 s, yielding a rate of roughly 20 documents/s. Subsequently, abstract retrieval was conducted in 678 s with 100% success, for a rate of 1.5 abstracts/s. Similar timings were obtained for equations that yielded larger and smaller corpus. ScopusLit stores the results in a single JSON format for portability and allows exporting the results in either CSV or Excel files for easier inspection. The file size for this case was 4.5 MB. ScopusLit allows a variety of bibliometric analyses based on the information stored in the JSON files. Basic ones include the citation count and the country distribution, as exemplified in Figs. 2 and 3. These two figures appear instantly on their corresponding tabs once an analysis is run.

Network analysis is another feature of ScopusLit. It performs cooccurrence networks of words, countries and authors. For this purpose, it extracts the affiliation_country, author_names and authkeywords fields from the Scopus metadata stored in the JSON files and leverages NetworkX Python library to create co-occurrence, co-authorship and Country collaboration networks. Users can define the minimum number of co-occurrences and maximum number of nodes. Fig. 4 displays the word co-occurrence network, which was generated with 6 minimum cooccurrences and 40 maximum nodes in 13.7 s on an Apple M4 Pro SoC,.

Previous figures were generated using the entire set of search results. ScopusLit allows result generation using filtered search results. Users can filter by year range, document types, countries and minimum citations. Fig. 5 show the results for keyword analysis -word cloud and evolution along time- when a filter is applied to consider journal articles and years between 2016 and 2026.

Based on the abstract retrieval, ScopusLit performs text analysis based on documents for which abstracts were downloaded. On the text analysis tab, the app indicated the number of abstracts available for the process. Word clouds (see Fig. 6), TF-IDF and topic analysis. For the latter, users can select either the NMF or LDA [13] techniques.(Fig. 7)

Fig. 7 shows the topic-word heatmap over the entire search results using NMF for 5 topics, which was generated by ScopusLit in 2 s. The LDA analysis yields almost identical results in 3 s. Users interpret the output by examining the top 10 weighted terms for each topic and the accompanying topic-word heatmap. The listed terms indicate the semantic content of each latent topic, while the heatmap shows the rela tive contribution of each term to each topic. The output should be interpreted as an exploratory thematic summary of the abstract corpus.

docs.title: 4. Impact
docs.text:
Bibliometric analysis is essential for literature reviews and is argu ably among the most transversal and interdisciplinary tool researchers have at their disposal. It has been applied across disciplines such as resource allocation [17], engineering education [18] and underground mining operations [19]. ScopusLit is an open-source tool that lowers the barrier to bibliometric analysis by integrating search, analysis, and visualization into a single browser-based interface with no programming requirement. This makes quantitative literature analysis accessible to researchers who lack programming skills or familiarity with specialized bibliometric software. Table 1 compares ScopusLit with established bibliometric tools across key functional dimensions.

Table 1 compares ScopusLit with established bibliometric tools using a functional criterion: a feature is marked as supported when it is available natively within the tool’s standard workflow, limited when it is available only for a narrower subset of outputs or with restricted customization, partial when it can be achieved through additional steps, scripts, or external packages, and not supported when it is not part of the tool’s documented workflow.

As shown in Table 1, ScopusLit’s main contribution is the native integration of Scopus query execution, abstract retrieval, bibliometric analysis, abstract-level text mining, search consolidation, and export within a single browser-based, zero-code interface. Established tool such as VOSviewer, Bibliometrix, CiteSpace, and Publish or Perish provide mature and widely used capabilities, particularly for science mapping, citation analysis, and bibliometric indicators. However, ScopusLit emphasizes a different use case: reducing manual transfers between platforms and supporting multi-query, Scopus-centered systematic review workflows from data retrieval to publication-ready outputs.

The tool enables reproducible bibliometric workflows. Each search is persisted as a JSON file that captures the query, execution date, full result set, and downloaded abstracts. This enables exact reproduction of analyses and facilitates sharing of bibliometric datasets between collaborators. The consolidation feature, with both union and comparison modes, directly supports the multi-query workflow typical of systematic reviews following the PRISMA methodology [9].

The inclusion of TF-IDF term extraction and topic modeling on full abstract corpora represents a capability not available in the most widely used bibliometric tools. This allows researchers to move beyond keyword-based analysis to identify latent thematic structures in the literature, which is particularly valuable for characterizing emerging or interdisciplinary research fields. From a practical standpoint, every visualization can be exported at 300 DPI, meeting the minimum resolution requirements of most scientific journals. The multi-sheet Excel export provides immediately usable supplementary materials for review articles.

docs.title: 5. Conclusions
docs.text:
This paper presented ScopusLit, an open-source, web-based appli cation for bibliometric analysis of scientific literature indexed in the

Scopus database. The tool is built on Python with Streamlit and pybliometrics, and provides a complete workflow from search execution through analysis and export without requiring programming knowledge from the user.

The key contributions of ScopusLit are the integration of API-based search, abstract retrieval, and analysis within a single zero-code interface; the incorporation of TF-IDF and topic modeling on abstracts; cooccurrence network analysis for keywords, authors, and countries; and the search consolidation feature with union and comparison modes supporting systematic review workflows. An illustrative example shows that ScopusLit can retrieve, store, analyze, and visualize a corpus of more than one thousand records using a reproducible JSON-based workflow. The results demonstrate the practical value of combining API-based retrieval with bibliometric indicators, co-occurrence networks, TF-IDF extraction, and topic modeling in one environment. A full workflow of document and abstract retrieval on a query of 1036 took <15 min, including figure generation and abstract topic modeling.

The main current limitation is the exclusive dependence on Scopus metadata and API access. As a result, ScopusLit does not yet support multi-database retrieval or advanced citation-based analyses such as cocitation and bibliographic coupling. From a software-development perspective a future direction is to transition ScopusLit from its current monolithic implementation toward a modular architecture, which would improve maintainability, facilitate testing, and encourage community-driven extensions and contributions.

docs.title: a b s t r a c t
docs.text:
A Systematic Mapping Study is an instrument frequently used to carry out a search process, identifi cation, and classification of studies in different fields. Researchers in front of this type of process have a challenge while managing the data about these studies. This paper presents a software tool that has been created to help those who need to build a systematic mapping study. In addition, this work follows the evidence-based software engineering approach and extends it through a software tool by including different ways of adapting this process.
