docs.title: Color artwork
docs.text:
If you submit usable color figures with your accepted article, we will ensure that they appear in color online.

Please ensure that color images are accessible to all, including those with impaired color vision. Learn more about color and web accessibility.

docs.title: Generative AI and Figures, images and other artwork
docs.text:
Please read our policy on the use of generative AI and AI-assisted tools in figures, images and artwork, which can be found in Elsevier’s GenAI Policies for Journals. This policy states:

  • AI tools may be used to support the creation of explanatory images (such as flow charts, conceptual diagrams, or schematic illustrations)

  • AI tools may be used to create data visualizations (such as plots, charts, graphs, or heatmaps) when the output is directly derived from underlying data using reproducible analytical, computational, or statistical methods.

AI tools must not be used to create or alter images that represent primary observed or experimental data (such as western blots, microscopy images, histology images, or patient images) that were not directly obtained in the research. This includes adjustments to brightness, contrast, or color balance, which should only be done using established image processing software.

This policy does not prevent the use of AI tools in formal research design or research methods (such as in AI-assisted imaging approaches used for collection and/or interpretation of the underlying research data or predictive modelling of clinical outcomes based on patient data).

Authors are responsible for ensuring the accuracy and originality of all images submitted for publication. If you used generative AI tools to create images in your manuscript, you should disclose this in each image caption as well as in the general Generative AI disclosure statement.

docs.title: Supplementary material
docs.text:
We encourage the use of supplementary materials such as applications, images and sound clips to enhance research. Some guidelines:

Supplementary material should be accurate and relevant to the research.

Cite all supplementary files in the manuscript text.

Submit all supplementary materials at the same time as your manuscript.

Include a concise, descriptive caption for each supplementary file, describing its content.

After submission supplementary files can only be added or replaced in the revision stage of the editorial process.

Be aware that all supplementary materials provided will appear online in the exact same way as received. These files will not be checked, formatted or typeset by the production team.

docs.title: Video
docs.text:
This journal accepts video material and animation sequences to support and enhance your scientific research. We encourage you to include links to video or animation files within articles. Some guidelines:

When including video or animation file links within your article, refer to the video or animation content by adding a note in your text where the file should be placed.

Clearly label files ensuring the given file name is directly related to the file content.

Provide files in one of our recommended file formats. Files should be within our preferred maximum file size of 150 MB per file, 1 GB in total.

Provide "stills" for each of your files. These will be used as standard icons to personalize the link to your video data. You can choose any frame from your video or animation or make a separate image.

Provide descriptive text in your manuscript to refer to the video content. This text helps ensure accessibility for visually impaired readers who rely on descriptive information. For journals publishing in print this is also essential, as video and animation files cannot be embedded in the print version.

We publish all video and animation files supplied in the electronic version of your article.

For more detailed instructions, we recommend that you read our guidelines on submitting video content to be included in the body of an article.

docs.title: Research data
docs.text:
We are committed to supporting the storage of, access to and discovery of research data, and our research data policy sets out the principles guiding how we work with the research community to support a more efficient and transparent research process.

Research data refers to the results of observations or experimentation that validate research findings, which may also include software, code, models, algorithms, protocols, methods and other useful materials related to the project.

Please read our guidelines on sharing research data for more information on depositing, sharing and using research data and other relevant research materials.

docs.title: Research data deposit, citation and linking
docs.text:
For this journal, Option C instructions from our research data guidelines apply. This means that you are required to:

Deposit your research data in a relevant data repository.

Cite and link to this dataset in your article.

If this is not possible, make a statement explaining why research data cannot be shared.

docs.title: Data statement
docs.text:
To foster transparency, you are required to state the availability of any data at submission.

Ensuring data is available may be a requirement of your funding body or institution. If your data is unavailable to access or unsuitable to post, you can state the reason why (e.g., your research data includes sensitive or confidential information such as patient data) during the submission process. This statement will appear with your published article on ScienceDirect.

Read more about the importance and benefits of providing a data statement.

docs.title: Data linking
docs.text:
Linking to the data underlying your work increases your exposure and may lead to new collaborations. It also provides readers with a better understanding of the described research.

docs.title: Co-submission of related data, methods or protocols
docs.text:
You are encouraged to publish a description of your research data, methods, or protocols related to your regular article as a cosubmission article in Data in Brief or MethodsX .

This co-submission can be submitted at the same time as your regular manuscript submission to this journal. If both your regular and co-submitted manuscripts are accepted for publication, they will be linked together on ScienceDirect, thereby promoting research reproducibility, interoperability, and open science.

  • Prepare a separate manuscript describing your research data, methods, or protocols using the mandatory templates from Data in Brief or in MethodsX .

  • Submit this co-submission alongside your regular manuscript as a separate submission item; on the ‘Attach files’ page in Editorial Manager, after which it will be automatically forwarded to the Data in Brief or MethodsX and assigned an editor.

For associated Article Processing Charge (APC) details, please visit:

docs.title: Journal specific information: Writing and formatting
Use of word processing software
docs.text:
It is important that the file be saved in the native format of the word processor used. The text should be in single-column format. Keep the layout of the text as simple as possible. Most formatting codes will be removed and replaced on processing the article. In particular, do not use the word processor's options to justify text or to hyphenate words. However, do use bold face, italics, subscripts, superscripts etc. When preparing tables, if you are using a table grid, use only one grid for each individual table and not a grid for each row. If no grid is used, use tabs, not spaces, to align columns. The electronic text should be prepared in a way very similar to that of conventional manuscripts (see also the Guide to Publishing with Elsevier). Note that source files of figures, tables and text graphics will be required whether or not you embed your figures in the text. See also the section on Electronic artwork.

To avoid unnecessary errors you are strongly advised to use the 'spell-check' and 'grammar-check' functions of your word processor. When preparing your manuscript, please make sure that you strictly adhere to the Template for Original Software Publications.

docs.title: Article sections
docs.text:
Divide your manuscript into clearly defined and numbered sections. Number subsections 1.1 (then 1.1.1, 1.1.2, ...), then 1.2, etc.

docs.title: Footnotes

You may use system features that automatically build footnotes into text. Alternatively, you can indicate the position of footnotes within the text and present them in a separate section at the end of your article.

docs.title: Acknowledgements

docs.title: Appendices
docs.text:
We ask you to use the following format for appendices:

Identify individual appendices within your article using the format: A, B, etc.

Give separate numbering to formulae and equations within appendices using formats such as Eq. (A.1), Eq. (A.2), etc. and in subsequent appendices, Eq. (B.1), Eq. (B. 2) etc. In a similar way, give separate numbering to tables and figures using formats such as Table A.1; Fig. A.1, etc.

docs.title: References within text
docs.text:
Any references cited within your article should also be present in your reference list and vice versa. Some guidelines:

References cited in your abstract must be given in full.

We recommend that you do not include unpublished results and personal communications in your reference list, though you may mention them in the text of your article.

Any unpublished results and personal communications included in your reference list must follow the standard reference style of the journal. In substitution of the publication date add "unpublished results" or "personal communication."

References cited as "in press" imply that the item has been accepted for publication.

Linking to cited sources will increase the discoverability of your research. We encourage the use of Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) as reference links, as they provide a permanent link to the electronic article referenced.

Before submission, check that all data provided in your reference list are correct, including any references which have been copied. Providing correct reference data allows us to link to abstracting and indexing services such as Scopus, Crossref and PubMed. Any incorrect surnames, journal or book titles, publication years or pagination within your references may prevent link creation.

docs.title: Reference style
docs.text:
Indicate references by number(s) in square brackets in line in the text. You can refer to author names within your text, but you must always give the reference number, e.g., "as demonstrated [3,6]. Barnaby and Jones [8] obtained a different result ....".

Number the references in the reference list in the order in which they appear in the text.

Please note the shortened form for last page number. e.g., 51-9, and that for more than 6 authors the first 6 should be listed followed by 'et al.'.

You can list web references separately under a new heading directly after your reference list or include them in your reference list.

docs.title: Software references
docs.text:
Cite software (including computational code, scripts, models, notebooks and libraries) in the same way as other sources of information to support proper attribution and credit, reproducibility, collaboration and reuse, and encourage building on the work of others to further research. To facilitate this, useful information is provided in this article on the essentials of software citation by FORCE 11, of which Elsevier is a member.

A reference to software should include the following elements:

  • Creator(s): the authors or project that developed the software.

  • Title: the name of the software.

  • Publication venue: the publication venue of the software, preferably, an archive or repository that provides permanent identifiers.

  • Date: the date the software was published. This is the date associated with a release or version of the software, or “n.d.” if the date is unknown.

  • Identifier: a resolvable pointer to the software, preferably, a PID that resolves to a landing page containing descriptive metadata about the software, similar to how a Digital Object Identifier (DOI) for a paper that points to a page about the paper rather than directly to a representation of the paper, such as the PDF. DOIs are preferable, and other examples of PIDs include Handles, RRIDs, ASCL IDs, swMath IDs, Software Heritage IDs, ARK Alliance, etc. If there is no PID for the software, a URL to where the software exists may be the best identifier available.

  • Version: the identifier for the version of the software being referenced. If the version is unidentified or unknown, the date of access should be used.

Type: some reference styles (e.g., APA), require a bracketed description of the citation (e.g., [Computer software]) to be included.

If an article exists that describes the software, it should be cited as an additional reference, as well as citing the software itself. Do not cite the article instead of the software.

docs.title: Preprint references
docs.text:
We ask you to mark preprints clearly. You should include the word "preprint" or the name of the preprint server as part of your reference and provide the preprint DOI.

Where a preprint has subsequently become available as a peer-reviewed publication, use the formal publication as your reference.

If there are preprints that are central to your work or that cover crucial developments in the topic, but they are not yet formally published, you may reference the preprint.

docs.title: Reference management software
docs.text:
Most journals have their reference template available in popular reference management software products. These include products that support Citation Style Language (CSL) such as Mendeley Reference Manager.

If you use a citation plug-in from these products, select the relevant journal template and all your citations and bibliographies will automatically be formatted in the journal style. We advise you to remove all field codes before submitting your manuscript to any reference management software product.

If a template is not available for this journal, follow the format given in examples in the reference style section of this Guide for Authors.

docs.title: 3.7. Performance metrics
docs.text:
To evaluate the accuracy and completeness of enriched metadata, we define two key metric categories: completeness metrics and quality status levels . These metrics help assess data coverage, track improvements through enrichment processes, and classify metadata quality based on missing information.

  • a) Completeness Metrics: Completeness metrics measure how well Field

  • metadata fields are populated and improved after enrichment. Coverage calculates the percentage of non-empty fields, indicating overall metadata completeness. API Enrichment Rate assesses how much the metadata quality improves after integration with external data sources. Merge Success Rate measures the percentage of records successfully combined without data loss or duplication. These indicators ensure that metadata enrichment processes effectively enhance data integrity.

  • b) Quality Status Levels: To classify metadata quality, we define six levels based on the percentage of missing data. Excellent (0% missing data) indicates fully complete records, while Very Good ( < 1%) represents minor gaps. Good ( < 5%) is considered acceptable for most analyses, whereas Acceptable ( < 20%) denotes moderate gaps. Poor ( < 50%) suggests significant missing information, and Critical (≥50%) indicates unreliable metadata that requires substantial improvement. These quality status levels provide a standardized framework for evaluating the reliability of enriched metadata.

docs.title: 3.8. Statistical reporting
docs.text:
The software generates detailed statistical summaries, including:

  • a) Duplication rates.

  • b) Metadata completeness ratios.

  • c) Quality metrics for enriched datasets.

  • d) API Based Enrichment field, source, value logs.

These reports help users assess the quality and reliability of their processed datasets.

docs.title: 3.9. Automation and workflow
docs.text:
The "DataProcessor" class is the primary access point for users, as it defines the pipeline phases and performs the automatic processing of bibliometric datasets. Users start the workflow with a single command: "python DataProcessor.py".

The pipeline assists users with project selection, optional API enrichment, and data processing. When finished, the outputs are saved in the specified project directory. Users can utilize these results for bibliometric analysis or further processing in programs such as VosViewer and Biblioshiny.

docs.title: 3.10. Time complexity of the framework
docs.text:
The time complexity of BibexPy’s framework is influenced by the size of the input datasets and the operations performed, such as deduplication and metadata enrichment. Key factors affecting time complexity include:

  • a) Scalability: The pipeline efficiently processes both small and large datasets.

  • b) API Integration: Metadata enrichment through API calls depends on the response times of external services.

  • c) Computational Efficiency: BibexPy is optimized for performance using efficient algorithms for deduplication and data transformation.

Overall, BibexPy balances computational efficiency with data quality, providing researchers with a scalable solution for bibliometric data preparation.

docs.title: 4. Illustrative examples
docs.text:
The BibexPy framework offers multiple ways for users to interact

with it, ensuring flexibility and ease of use. These options include:

  • a) Command-Line Interface (CLI): The command-line interface is the principal interaction technique, allowing users to run the software with minimal effort. Listing 1 shows an example of using the CLI to process bibliometric datasets. Users launch the main script (python DataProcessor.py) and follow the prompts to choose a project, set up metadata enrichment, and generate output.

  • b) Python API: Advanced users can use BibexPy’s modular architecture to directly access its classes and methods from Python programs. This enables greater flexibility and integration with other workflows.

  • c) Script-Based Customization : The most flexible method to use BibexPy is to create short Python scripts that make use of its modular components. This technique enables greater customization and experimentation with other workflows.

Listing 2 is an example of a Python script that shows how to use BibexPy to process bibliometric datasets. The script begins by loading the essential modules from BibexPy, which prepares the environment for data processing. The first stage is loading and merging datasets from Web of Science and Scopus into a single format using the DataImporter class.

The next step is deduplication, which uses the Deduplicator module to remove redundant items based on DOI matches. The script then uses the MetadataEnricher class to add missing properties like abstracts, author affiliations, and citation counts via API.

Finally, the FormatConverter module changes the data to a format that VosViewer and Biblioshiny can understand. The script automates every stage of bibliometric data preparation, resulting in a clean, enhanced dataset that is ready for analysis. This programmatic method allows researchers to construct custom workflows, adjust parameters, and expand the pipeline to meet specific bibliometric study objectives.

docs.title: 5. Impact
docs.text:
BibexPy has cleared the path for comprehensive bibliometric research by enabling the rapid integration and processing of datasets from many sources, including Web of Science and Scopus. This capacity enables academics to investigate problems that were previously restricted by the limitations of manual data preparation, such as mapping research patterns across disciplines, assessing worldwide citation networks, and finding emergent study areas across domains [23,24]. By automating data integration, deduplication, and metadata enrichment, BibexPy facilitates the pursuit of current research issues [25–27]. It improves the reliability and comprehensiveness of bibliometric datasets, ensuring that analyses are based on high-quality data, and decreases preprocessing time dramatically, allowing researchers to focus on interpretation and insight generation.

Although BibexPy is in its early stages of development, significant efficiency gains have been observed in initial tests with sample datasets. The results obtained in these tests clearly demonstrate the software’s impact and potential in bibliometric data preparation processes. As the software becomes more widely known and adopted, download statistics, citations in academic publications, and feedback from the user community will provide more comprehensive evidence of BibexPy’s impact.

docs.title: 1. Introduction
docs.text:
Buhos responds to the need for a software tool that manages the complete process of systematic literature reviews (SLR) of medium to high complexity in the fields of social science and education, fields which have their particular requirements, distinct from those of other knowledge domains. Upon analyzing the results of the Kohl et al. review [1] on software tools that partially or fully cover the stages of an SLR, it is observed that most of these tools have been designed with the health and medical sciences and software engineering in mind, albeit being promoted as tools for general use. SLRs designed from the perspective of these disciplines share characteristics that do not necessarily fill the requirements of other fields of knowledge.

In the health and medical sciences (HMS) the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [2] is predominantly used to direct the performance of systematic reviews. Most of its indications are related to the evaluation of clinical assays and randomized clinical trials (RCT) as these are considered to deliver more reliable evidence than other types of investigations. The focus on a specific type of investigation enables the establishment of a review procedure that is relatively consistent, standardized, with defined steps, independently of the specific research question [3]. It is common practice to screen and extract information from thousands of articles. The process can be partially automated [4,5], as there are clear criteria for defining research questions, such as the well-known PICOS — participants, interventions, comparisons, outcomes and study design [6]. For performing quality assessments, the Cochrane manual offers a detailed analysis of the possible bias risks, including a domain-based tool for their assessment [2].

The focus for conducting SLRs and meta-analysis in the ambit of social science is fundamentally different from that of HMS. The need exists to incorporate diverse types of investigations into the SLR, such as observational studies and case studies, as RCTs are infrequent. In fact, it is not possible to conduct RCTs on certain topics for ethical reasons [3,7]. It must be taken into consideration that observational studies cannot be evaluated in as standardized and step-by-step a manner as are RCTs [3]. Depending on the research question, the sources of bias must be carefully assessed in each study, considering the latter’s specific design, and carrying out a historical, theoretical and contextualized assessment [7,8]. Thus, a software tool for conducting SLRs in the social sciences should be able to record in detail the search procedures, the justification for using moderators, the coding procedures and agreements between independent coders, seeking the greatest possible transparency in evaluating the quality of the studies considered [8]. Besides this,

the tool must have the capability to accept different types of information sources, since most of the evidence is not found in journals but in grey literature, such as conferences, theses, technical reports and other unpublished documents [9].

Therefore, developing an SLR-supporting software tool for the social sciences requires unifying various types of investigations, theoretical as well as empirical, in order to reach a conclusion. The software tool utilized must be a flexible one that enables multiple ways of performing systematic reviews, while ensuring maximum transparency and rigor by recording each step followed by each evaluator, especially in discrepancy resolution [10].

The studies carried out in the software engineering (SE) environment on user requirements for SLR support software [11,12] are pertinent for software development geared to the social sciences, since both disciplines pose similar challenges vis à vis SLR development. This is because the research designs utilized are generally of an observational and post-facto nature, and the participants’ profile is usually that of experts, making it difficult to establish blind procedures [13]. Considering the main requirements described in the literature, Buhos incorporates several tools to facilitate communication between users, which, added to its ability to handle large numbers of documents in a robust manner, enables the performance of medium- to large-scale SLRs. Besides this, metadata and files of already finished documents can be reused to update prior reviews. With regard to software development processes, special attention has been given to the application’s usability, test coverage, maintainability and documentation.

docs.title: 2.1. Systematic literature review: the concept
docs.text:
Literature reviews are investigations that seek to ‘‘describe, summarize, evaluate, clarify, and/or integrate the content of the primary reports’’ [14, (p107)] within a specific area of knowledge, in its empirical, theoretical, critical or methodological aspects. The considerable ambiguity imbedded in the concept of ‘literature review’ has led to significant efforts to define its precise meaning [9], with 16 to 27 different types identified [15–17] depending on the classification system employed. In any case, there is consensus that the Systematic Literature Review (SLR) is the most precise and reliable method for obtaining information [18], having demonstrated its usefulness for both theoretical and empirical approaches [19]. It has had notable success in the areas of HMS [20], software engineering [21,22], social sciences [7,23] and education [24].

The concept of SLR can be understood either specifically or comprehensively. The definition of SLR adopted by the Cochrane

C. Bustos Navarrete et al. / SoftwareX 7 (2018) 360–372

362

Collaboration, associated to the manner in which it is carried out in the HMS, indicates that the SLR ‘‘attempts to collate all empirical evidence that fits pre-specified eligibility criteria in order to answer a specific research question. It uses explicit, systematic methods that are selected with a view to minimizing bias, thus providing more reliable findings from which conclusions can be drawn and decisions made’’ [2, (sec1.2.2)]. An SLR must have the following characteristics: (a) clear objectives, with preselected criteria for including or excluding articles; (b) an explicit, reproducible methodology; (c) systematic search capability that attempts to identify all studies that meet the inclusion and exclusion criteria; (d) an assessment of the validation of the evidence contained in the studies included through bias risk assessment, for example, and (e) a systematic presentation and synthesis of the evidence collected [2]. These revisions are usually associated with metaanalysis, which applies statistical methods to summarize the results. Meta-analysis is used to synthesize the evidence presented in the different studies incorporated into the SLR to detect effects, estimate their magnitude and variability, and analyze the factors that influence them [25].

From a broader perspective, an SLR is considered as a review of the literature that is exhaustive, transparent and unbiased, developed with a clearly defined methodology, performed in a systematic manner [26]. This is what differentiates it from a narrative review, which mixes theories and opinions and does not apply a specific method of selection and assessment to the available information [27]. An example of this mode of understanding systematic reviews is put forward by EPPI-Centre, which explicitly points out that the only thing that differentiates a systematic review from one that is not systematic is that ‘‘a systematic review has an explicit, rigorous methodology. This makes the results of the review accountable and open to criticism and debate’’ [28, (p9)].

docs.title: 2.2. Stages of a systematic review
docs.text:
According to the guidelines of Kitchenham & Charters [13], the systematic review process can be divided into three major phases: planning, conducting, and reporting. Each of these phases in turn consists of various stages. Planning the review considers: (a) identifying the need for conducting a review, (b) commissioning of the study to an external party, (c) specifying the research question(s), (d) developing the protocol, and (e) evaluation of the protocol by an external agent. Performing the review involves (a) identifying the studies through an adequate search strategy, (b) selection of the studies, (c) evaluating the quality of the studies, (d) extracting information from the studies and monitoring the process, and (e) synthesizing the information. Finally, the report involves: (a) specifying the dissemination mechanism, (b) formatting the report, and (c) evaluating the report. All these stages are considered mandatory, except for commissioning the study, evaluating the protocol and the evaluation of the final report.

It should be kept in mind that the review process is considered as being iterative, thus it is possible that, for instance, the protocol will be refined following its evaluation, or that the methods of analysis planned will be improved once the data is obtained [13]. Snowballing is an iteration-based method for identifying pertinent studies not yielded by database searches. There are two modalities: (a) forward-snowballing: new documents are incorporated that cite previously selected documents, (b) backward-snowballing: adds documents cited in the selected documents. This method is particularly useful when a critical mass of papers has already been identified [29].

2.3. SLR in health and medical sciences, software engineering and

social sciences

The greatest developments in SLR have been observed in the fields of health care and health policy. It is hoped that by the end of the decade of the 2010s, over 200,000 SLRs will have become available to HMS [25]. In the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO), there has been a ten-fold increase in the number of SLRs between 2012 and 2017, from 63 per month in 2012 to 800 per month in 2017 [18].

SLRs in the fields of health and medicine owe their success to their association with evidence-based medicine (EBM), defined as ‘‘the sensible use of the best available external evidence from systematic research, assimilated with individual clinical expertise to evaluate the best course of care for a patient’’ [20, (p2)] The search for evidence can be very difficult for physicians, considering the staggering volume of research data available on Internet. The existence of publication bias renders it even more difficult to reach a precise assessment of the evidence [30]; thus the critical role of the systematic review, which evaluates the available evidence in a systematic, reproducible manner, at the same time weighing the risk of bias [20]. For this reason, SLRs are routinely used by researchers to inform on health practices and policies [31].

SLRs in HMS are significantly associated with the Cochrane Database on Systematic Reviews, which is a set of reviews and protocols maintained by specialized groups [20]. The two basic principles of the Cochrane Collaboration are the need for unbiased comparison of different interventions, which is the reason for their preference for SLR in RCTs, as well as the importance of ongoing selection and updating of the available evidence, to arrive at the most reliable estimators of the effects [32]. Clarity in the type of studies, as well as in the analyses considered to be appropriate, enables establishing a standardized procedure for performing the SLR with step-by-step instructions, as reflected in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [2].

In software engineering (SE), the introduction of SLRs in the discipline [33,34] is considered to have occurred in 2004 due to their central role in evidence-based software engineering (EBSE) presented by Kitchenham et al. [35], which sought to integrate academic research and industrial practice in order to find the best evidence sustaining the software development. Kitchenham proposes a procedure for conducting SLRs in software engineering [36], which was updated in 2007, applying concepts from the social sciences [13], and in 2013, following a tertiary study of 63 SLRs in the discipline [29].

SE investigation poses specific challenges that are analogous to those of research in the social sciences. First, in HMS it is common to restrict an SLR to RCTs or, considering the research question, specific designs can be pinpointed as being more appropriate. In the case of SE, the paucity of empirical research implies aggregating information from a wide variety of different types of research [13]. In addition, the SE techniques studied in SLR are usually part of a larger software development cycle, which makes it difficult to observe an individual effect. Unlike studies conducted in HMS, where treatment recipients can be blind to the interventions performed, in SE the methods and techniques usually must be developed by experts [37].

While the development of SLRs in SE has not been as explosive as in the health area, it is nonetheless a very active area of development, characterized by a concern for finding software tools that can support SLR processes, and by the presence of multiple tertiary studies aimed at exploring both the adoption of these types of studies as well as the evidence on specific themes. In 2017, a mapping study on threats to validity reported the existence of 316 SLRs in the area of software engineering [38]. Multiple investigations have examined the use of tools in SLR, conducting evaluations of their

C. Bustos Navarrete et al. / SoftwareX 7 (2018) 360–372

363

characteristics [1,11,39,40] and identifying the requirements and characteristics that the SE community expected from them [12, 41,42]. Multiple tertiary studies have been conducted to evaluate the adoption, quality and use of SLRs in the discipline [22,43], the experience of conducting SLRs [29,33] and evaluating the evidence on specific themes such as Ambient Assisted Living [44], Agile development [45], Software process improvement [46], Software testing [47], requirements engineering [48] global software development [49] and distributed software development [50].

As for the social sciences, various challenges are posed by SLRs. First of all, while there is already a long tradition of systematic reviews in social science, the incorporation of quantitative tools developed in the health environment has clashed with the more qualitative tradition in evidence gathering, particularly in the field of education [51]. Secondly, much of the available evidence is based on observational designs, which required undertaking the significant methodological effort of defining the conditions under which unbiased results could be obtained [3]. In HMS, SLRs and meta-analysis focus on establishing homogeneous evidence which enables establishing each treatment’s efficacy with certainty for wide, hopefully worldwide dissemination. In contrast, the social sciences focus on describing the heterogeneity of populations and situations to understand the causal processes that are the basis of a specific intervention’s successful outcome. For example, the representativity of a study population can be more important, or how much information is available on confounding variables, than the presence or absence of randomization. Besides this, there are different reporting styles even within each discipline, adding complexity to the task of standardizing the information to be gathered [7].

Regarding the orientations for the performance of SLRs in the social sciences, there are important differences in approach, depending on the discipline and the institutions sponsoring the studies [3]. In the field of education, the What Works Clearinghouse, a flagship product of the Institute of Education Sciences at the U.S. Department of Education, strongly emphasizes quantitative analysis of RCT and quasi-experimental design, with rigorous criteria for inclusion and exclusion [16], which brings it more in line with the Cochrane approach. The Campbell Collaboration has focused on the effectiveness of programs, policies and practices in the fields of crime and justice, education, international development, and social welfare. Notwithstanding the recognition of the importance of RCTs, it is considered advisable to include studies with designs having less internal but greater external validity, and to add qualitative studies that allow for increasing the review’s explicative capacity [32]. Finally, EPPI-Centre has focused on social policy, including education, health, social care, developing economies, sports, the environment and crime. It has a broad definition of what constitutes a review, considering aggregative approaches that seek to summarize information from different studies, such as meta-analyses, as well as configurative approaches involving an interpretative process of the information that is available for producing high-level explanations [28].

Considering the variety of existing approaches for carrying out systematic reviews in the social sciences, it is difficult to establish a clear indicator for demonstrating its scope. A search in Scopus of all documents in Social Sciences containing the terms ‘‘systematic review’’ or ‘‘meta-analysis’’ in their titles with different variations, and excluding those classified under the category of Medicine, lists a total of 10,100 documents, the majority from Psychology (4,679) followed by Business, Management and Accounting (1,754).

docs.title: 2.4. The role of software tools in SLR
docs.text:
Systematic literature review processes are difficult to execute. They require searching for hundreds of thousands of articles and

identifying which ones are useful. This entails meticulously recording a great deal of information on each document. The review process consists of several steps — prepare the topic, search for articles, screen studies, extract data, analyze and synthesize the data, then report findings [4]. Each step must be performed accurately, transparently, and recorded [13]. The selection of tools, particularly the IT tools, requires balancing initial and maintenance costs to achieve the necessary functionality in processes having differing degrees and levels of complexity [52].

The most important studies on the requirements of SLR users in reference to available computer tools are those of Al-Zubidy et al. [12] and Marshall et al. [11]. The Al-Zubidy study [12] conducted with SE practitioners, concludes that multiple requirements exist for SLR tools. It identifies 112, and that no tool is actually available at this time that covers them all. After analyzing 6 tools, the study found that each one covered from 32% to 68% of the community’s requirements. Most notable were the need for facilitated collaboration among participants located locally as well as in different countries, the need for reductions in researchers’ work time through automated processes, for access to a central repository with information from past SLRs, and for integration of the different tools. Marshall et al. [11] found that researchers who perform SLR in the social and health sciences agree with SE researchers on the importance of management of large-scale SLRs and the handling of communications within the team. They also placed special emphasis on the challenges that arise during processes of searching, selection and screening, and quality assessment. Differences are observed between social science and health science researchers with respect to SE researchers, in that the first require version control in SLRs and the option of formatting the references in the final report. In addition, social science researchers assign greater value to the possibility of carrying out meta-analyses, having access to safety mechanisms to maintain data confidentiality, while text analysis tools are less of a concern.

It should be emphasized that, while SLR tools can help speed up the process and perform actions that are extremely difficult or impossible for humans to do, they can only assist researchers in conducting the SLR, because human judgment is required at all stages of the process. While proposals exist for automating most [4,5] or the entire SLR process [53], this is only possible with a defined procedure and standardized quality criteria, which are proper only to HMS. More specifically, in the social sciences, the planning phase involves a process of negotiation between the researchers, practitioners and stakeholders, which, while possible to facilitate with computer tools, must necessarily be carried out by the individuals concerned [28]. In SE, however, and to a greater extent in the social sciences [7], the need for integrating various types of investigation for different situations implies the impossibility of applying a single quality criterion, as each study must be individually assessed on the basis of its context [8]. Finally, researchers need to have confidence in the reliability of automation mechanisms before they will accept them completely [11].

docs.title: 2.5. Related work
docs.text:
Multiple types of software are available for use in the performance of systematic reviews. There are programs that, while not designed to carry out systematic reviews, provide support for the various stages of the process. Office automation software, such as Microsoft Word or Excel, is useful for creating forms that can be replied to on paper or through e-mail. Web-based systems of forms and surveys generate forms that are simple to answer and process. While these programs are easy to setup and do not require much training to learn to use, they make it harder to keep a record of the project’s progress and resolve possible conflicts between evaluators [52].

C. Bustos Navarrete et al. / SoftwareX 7 (2018) 360–372

364

Of the commonly-employed research tools, reference management software is one of the most popular [54] with EndNote as the preferred choice of many researchers for supporting the search process [55,56], screening [57,58] and to eliminate duplication [59]. For the stage of data extraction, qualitative analysis software such as NVivo can be used [29,56,60].

Among the software tools designed to perform reviews are those that focus on specific stages of the process. According to Marshall & Brereton’s mapping study [40] out of 14 software tools, 11 concentrate on the conducting phase of the systematic review, particularly the search stage, data synthesis and data extraction. For the search stage, there are available tools such as EndNote; however, the main problem with them is that they are closed [53]. There is interest in accelerating the processes of screening and data extraction through partial automation using machine learning [4], with such tools as abstrackr [61], PEx [62], ExaCT [63], SwiftReview [64] y GAPScreener [65]. Rayyan is a free tool for use in the initial stages of planning, search and screening, that offers the great advantage of having a highly usable web interface and mobile application. [66]. Another similar open source code tool is CREBP-SRA, which is mainly focused on reference and search management, and secondarily, on the screening process [67]. For the analysis and report stage, RevMan stands out for its capabilities in the preparation of protocols and articles, the development of meta-analyses and presentation of graphic results [68].

At the end of this list are the software applications that support the full process of systematic review. They enable carrying out searches, screening, data extraction, as well as numeric and qualitative analyses. A complete, updated summary of 22 of these tools is available in Kohl et al. [1], and so we will focus only on tools that consider two or more phases of the systematic review that are open source, as well as on those that are gratis or paid and not specifically assigned to the HMS.

We found 7 free code tools that support at least two of the three phases of a systematic review (see Table 1). All of these tools cover the conducting stage, 6 consider reports and 5, planning. Three of the tools, REviewER [69], SLRTool [70] and Slurp [55] can be considered as discontinued because they have not shown further development since at least 2015. All of the tools with the exception of REviewER and metagear are web-based. Notably, at least 4 of the tools come from software engineering, although two claim to be useful for other disciplines. With respect to the development stack used, the use of Python stands out in various combinations with other languages, as the most complex Colandr [71] tool. Complete information for developers is only available for HAWC [72] and for metagear [73]. The tool most similar to Buhos out of all those available is Parsifal [74], as it is web-based, covers all the stages of the SLR process, it meets the requirements of Software engineering which are proximate to the social sciences, allows carrying out reviews by multiple users, shows a high degree of usability, and is in active development. However, it does not have a system of permissions for controlling access to the platform, it does not have a permanent repository of documents that enables online quality assessment and data extraction.

The great majority of non-open source tools available for the performance of SLR that pertain to the social sciences are webbased. EPPI-Reviewer [75] is widely used as it is free to use and offers strong support for synthesis; however, it is specific to the health area and does not allow the performance of quality checks [55], it is not open source and cannot be used locally [76]. DistillerSR [77], according to its authors, is the most popular tool for performing systematic outlines with its powerful features of semiautomatic deduplication and screening. Nevertheless, it cannot be used locally and the subscription cost is prohibitive. JBI Sumari [78] has default support for 10 types of reviews in health, social sciences and the humanities, as well as a user role system with differentiated access. But it does not allow for the creation of custom

data extraction or quality assessment forms. Furthermore, access is limited to users with subscriptions. CADIMA [1] stands out for its highly structured interface, designed to guide review processes in a collaborative, intuitive way, its capacity for incorporating information extracted off-line and the option it offers of communicating the progress of the SLR in its website. However, it is not equipped with incorporated search or quantitative synthesis tools. SESRA [79] considers the complete SLR process, according to the phases and stages of Kitchenham & Charters [13], and is available in English and Portuguese. The developers have conducted objective and subjective evaluations of this tool and plan to expand it to cover SRL requirements in other disciplines.

A limited number of SLR tools is available off-line. SLR-Tool [80] is a free use Java-based tool, available in Spanish and English. Its main limitation is that it is not enabled for collaborative work. StArt [81,82] is a freeware alternative that provides a high degree of support for SLR user requirements [12], particularly through its capacity for enabling collaborative work and backward-snowballing. However, it is not open-code and can only be used in the operating system Windows.

docs.title: 2.6. Rationale for Buhos development
docs.text:
Thus, while there are tools available for managing the systematic review process in its entirety, most are not open source and are optimized solely for biomedical and software engineering research. From the perspective of our experience in systematic reviews in the fields of social science and education, a software tool is needed that can record each step of the process, including each researcher’s communications and decisions. It must have a defined methodology with clear stages, one that is adaptable to the research objectives as needed. In addition, the software must be easy to install, be available in multiple languages, and be possible to use both locally and online on various platforms. This will enable the development of accurate systematic reviews in the most efficient manner possible, within a broad range of scientific domains.

In terms of the SLR user requirements reported in the literature [11,12], Buhos facilitates the communication between the review users, providing an internal messaging and comments system for the document at each phase of the review process. This, in addition to the capability for managing hundreds of references swiftly, enables Buhos to support medium and large-scale SLRs. Special attention has been given to document storage, which allows reusing both metadata and article files between different SLRs. The security system implemented assigns specific roles for each user within the system and is of particular importance to social science researchers. For example, it enables permission to be granted solely for accessing the review results and not the review process or the original documents.

Regarding the software development processes, what sets Buhos apart is its high level of usability, testability and documentation. In our preliminary tests, the users learned to administer the tool and perform the steps for conducting an SLR within approximately one hour. Great user satisfaction was also observed with the interface innovations aimed at maximizing efficiency, such as the dashboard and the online PDF file viewer. As for testability, we have given special attention to complying with good engineering practices related to the test-driven development paradigm that guides the development of Buhos. Each new functionality includes specific tests allowing self-verification of correct functioning, together with the practice of Continuous Integration to enable rapid detection of problems. This renders the software fully functional at each iteration of development. Finally, Buhos includes extensive documentation for users and for developers. Users are provided with a manual with information on the SLR process and user

365

The authors consider that free and open source software (FOSS) offers two significant advantages for SLR support software development: efficiency and control. With respect to efficiency, the evidence indicates that with sufficient community participation, software can be generated that will fully satisfy the requirements of different user types and yield a lower error rate than equivalent proprietary software [83,84]. And as for control, according to the FOSS model, tools should be kept under the control of the user, whether individual or collective, which is compatible with the ethos of voluntary collaboration and academic autonomy that is proper to researchers [83].

Maintaining control over tools and data in such a costly process as an SLR is not merely an ethical issue; it is a practical one as well. While the notion of free use tools for developing SLR is an attractive one, users are well advised to consider the risk/benefit ratio aspect of vendor lock-in, particularly in relation to possible difficulties in information extraction from the application that might crop up, whether of processing data on other software programs or in the eventuality of switching to a different application if the first one turns out to be deficient or inadequate [85]. In the case of proprietary offline tools, while they provide greater control over the application and data, should any major problem with the software arise, the researcher remains in a situation of virtually total dependence on the developer, particularly if the data is recorded in non-standard ways.

docs.title: 3.1. Software architecture
docs.text:
Buhos is a web-based application in the client–server mode. The server can run on the same system that the user runs, or they can communicate over a computer network. Access to the system resources is done following the REST architectural style. This involves providing a uniform interface for accessing and manipulating the system’s resources, where each resource and the related actions are equipped with their own internal resource identifier. This will facilitate the maintenance of stateless communication, favoring visibility, reliability and scalability of the software [86].

The application runs on an HTTP server and is based on a Model – View – Controller pattern (MVC). It separates the code accessing the database and performs actions within the problem domain (Model) from that which submits the information to the user (View), and from that which accepts the user’s entries, coordinating models and the views (the Controller).

The model data is stored in an SQL database. The technique of Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) allowed access to the database information, using object-oriented programming. In addition, a database abstraction layer enabled the use of different databases according to the review requirements.

docs.title: 3.2. Software functionalities
docs.text:
The main features of Buhos Software are:

  • Multiplatform: Installers are provided for the Ubuntu, CentOS and Windows operating systems using source code. The application can run on any operating system in which Ruby 2.4 can be compiled.

  • Collaborative Work: A team develops each systematic review under the guidance of an administrator. An internal messaging system is provided to maximize transparency in the decision process.

  • Internationalization: All system texts and messages are available for translation, which enables adapting the software to various languages. Complete versions in English and Spanish are currently available.

  • Flexible Stages of Analysis: The work of systematic review is performed in stages — searching, screening the title and abstract, screening references (backward snowballing in the literature [29]) , full-text review and reporting. Searches or documents can be specifically allocated to each user at each stage, and the administrator decides which documents will be part of the following stage. New information can be incorporated in preceding stages and is automatically updated in subsequent stages.

  • Integration with various scientific metadata systems: The system allows recording searches exported from various bibliographic databases – currently WoS, Scopus, Ebscohost and Scielo – as well as references available in bibliographic reference software, using BibTeX. There is strong integration with Crossref and PubMed, enabling deduplication of records through DOI and/or PMID and obtaining information from references. Finally, the Scopus database can be contacted to obtain information on articles and their authors with a Scopus API key.

  • File Repository: Each systematic review can host different files, which may or may not be allocated to the corresponding documents. An online PDF and ODF file view is provided, for evaluation of the article’s quality as well as for data extraction, so that the entire process can be carried out online.

  • Multiple Forms of Analysis: The system considers the personalized definition of inclusion and exclusion criteria and of the criteria for evaluating the quality of the studies. Each document can be tagged using free or pre-established categories, and comments can be made on the inclusion and exclusion decisions at each stage as well. At the full-text review stage, a standardized form is incorporated to unify the reviewers’ analyses of the texts in each document, as well as the references to other articles.

  • Multiple Outputs: The list of records in each stage can be exported as a BibTeX or Excel file. The list of documents and their relationships can be exported in GraphML for analysis in network programs such as Gephi or yEd. A PRISMA flow diagram is also provided, which breaks down the information flow during the various stages of the process [6].

docs.title: 4.2. Evaluation of Buhos
docs.text:
We have evaluated the software Buhos considering three criteria. The first criterion was usability. Buhos was used in a simplified SLR process by 5 participants who had wide experience in conducting SLR, but had no prior contact with the application. The second criterion was the extent to which Buhos satisfied the requirements of SLR users in the SE field, assessed by using the method described by Al-Zubidy et al. [12]. The third criterion was coverage of tests and maintainability. This was evaluated by using the metrics in the website Code Climate.

The Buhos software usability test aimed to determine whether the participants were capable of using Buhos to conduct an SLR. Usability requirements and problems were identified and an assessment made of the software’s perceived level of usability. The test was held with 5 individuals who were experts in using SLR, 3 of them in the field of psychology and 2 in economics. Given the participants’ time constraints, a one-hour protocol was applied individually, involving the performance of a complete SLR, which included simulated journal articles. In the course of the activity, a Think Aloud protocol was followed in which each person described what he or she thought of the application while interacting with it. Upon completing the task, they answered a questionnaire that included questions on sociodemographic variables, experience in carrying out SLR and using the System Usability Scale [98], which is a robust usability scale having broad empirical support [99]. Since all of the participants spoke Spanish, a translation used in a previous study was employed [100].

All of the participants successfully carried out the complete SLR procedure with an average time of 64.6 min (SD = 19.36). Through thematic analysis [101], 12 usability problems were identified and 17 different suggestions were made. Three bugs were also detected and immediately corrected following application of each procedure. The main difficulty observed was the lack of a link that allowed the user to go back to a previous step in different interfaces. The SUS questionnaire yielded an average score of 86.5 (DE = 8.4). Using the adjective range scale of Bangor, Kortum & Miller [99], this average would indicate that the software is rated on average ‘Excellent’; the minimum score of 72.5 is equivalent to ‘Good’. A detailed description methodology and results is available in attached dataset (DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.17632/kjn9ggxhwz. 1#file-3d76b410-d18f-404f-b7ee-7c9faf18e273).

The process based on DISSMET methodology used by Al-Zubidy et al. [12] was used to evaluate Buhos’ suitability vis à vis SLR user requirements in the field of SE. A rating system of Full (1 point), Partial (0.5 points) and None (0 points) was applied to

the software tool’s coverage of 53 detailed requirements. The 53 requirements are divided into 11 consolidated groupings. Each consolidated group score is the average of the coverage scores of the detailed requirements making up the group. The overall coverage score is equivalent to the weighted mean of the consolidated requirement scores, obtained by assigning a weight from 10 to 1, according to the order of importance in which the original study users ranked each requirement coverage. A conservative rating system was used, in which Buhos was only rated as having full coverage of a detailed requirement if it provided as many as or more functions than the other software tools evaluated in the original study. Evaluation of each detailed requirement is available in attached dataset (DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.17632/kjn9ggxhwz. 1#file-9d75f890-6a8e-49e5-9ee3-0225daf0f613)

Table 2 presents summarized results of the requirements analysis for Buhos. There is full coverage in Buhos for Collaboration Support y Data Maintenance, and high level of coverage for Traceability. It should be considered that there is at least partial coverage of requirements in all areas. Although the overall coverage score is lower than that of StArt (68%), it is comparable to those of tools such as SESRA (59%) and Parsifal (63%), and much higher than those of SluRP (48%), SLRTool (44%) and SLR-Tool (32%). Thus, while Buhos was not designed to meet the SLR requirements in SE, it offers a degree of requirements coverage similar to those of other available tools.

Buhos has been developed according to the methodology of Test-driven development (TDD), wherein the developer must build an automated unit test in the form of assertions to define the requirements before writing the appropriate code. This implies that software development is iterative and goes through cycles of testing, development and refactoring [102]. Evidence exists that the code produced with this methodology is of better quality in terms of fewer errors, in experimental studies [103] and in case studies [104], although the development time window is longer and expertise is required to achieve the desired outcomes [105]. In terms of TDD implementation, Buhos has multiple unit tests and automated integration tests that use RSpec [106]. The software development follows the continuous integration model, in which automated local testing is done before committing, and testing each commit pushed to Github on an independent server through Travis CI (https://travis-ci.org/clbustos/buhos).

Buhos yields good indicators when its code coverage and maintainability metrics are analyzed. According to the information available in Code Climate (https://codeclimate.com/github/clbust os/buhos), Buhos’ test coverage is higher than 90%. Code Climate’s static code analysis indicates that Buhos has Category A maintainability, as shown by the minimal number of duplications and excessively long methods. There is no evidence of test coverage in other software tools except for Parsifal, in which the set of unitary tests shows 41% coverage.

docs.title: 5. Illustrative example
docs.text:
We offer three examples to demonstrate the capabilities of Buhos. Firstly, the Quick User Guide included in the User Manual (http://www.buhos.org/manual/en) is available as a tutorial entitled Video 1. The complete version is in http://www.buhos.org/ videos.

Secondly, a description is provided of how Buhos was used to carry out the first literary review process using then-existing software tools for SLR. And finally, an example of how to carry out Backward Snowballing, automated using Watir, is provided. A screencast of the process is available, entitled Video 2.

docs.title: 5.1. Revision of SLR support software
docs.text:
The systematic review documented in this paper, relative to software pertinent for developing systematic reviews, was performed through Buhos. The SLR team was made up of three members: one administrator and two analysts. The objectives of SLR were: (1) Identify software used to perform SLR (2) Describe the SLR software, detailing in which stages it would be used and the objectives to be accomplished, and (3) Identify the features required for SLR software. The process began with the creation of the systematic review, defining its objectives, inclusion and exclusion criteria, temporal extension and approach. A personalized form was generated consisting of two fields, one to capture information on the names of the tools, their uses and objectives, and another for the features required for the SLR software.

In the search stage, queries were incorporated made in different bibliographic bases (Scopus, Ebscohost y WoS), exported to BibTeX, as well as an informal search on Google, which was exported from Mendeley. Each search was recorded with information on the date, search text, description and the corresponding export file. All searches were validated, checking that at least information about title, year, authors and abstract were complete for each record.

In the stages that followed (titles and abstract screening, reference screening and full-text review), it was agreed by the team that two analysts should decide on the inclusion or exclusion of each document, based on the SLR objectives and the inclusion and exclusion criteria. The administrator would need to resolve whether each document should be included or not in the following stage. Fig. 3 shows the evaluators’ screening interface, which allows the analyst to include the inclusion and exclusion criteria that were applied, and add tags and a comment to inform the administrator of the decisions taken.

For the screening stage using title and abstract, the administrator assigned to the analysts the review of the 84 documents obtained from the search stage. Both analysts selected 21 documents as useful and 56 as irrelevant; for 7 documents the result was one vote of approval and another of rejection, and these were discarded by the administrator.

For the next stage of reference screening, all available information must be obtained on the references cited in the included documents. Most records imported through Scopus and WoS contained information on references, but not all; records imported through Mendeley did not include this information. The administrator proceeded to download the information available in Crossref for each document included in the screening stage, using the title and the abstract, on the administration platform. 302 references contained enough information to be incorporated as canonical documents. 27 documents were found to have two or more references in the texts selected during the previous stage, with 9 deemed relevant by both analysts using their titles and abstracts. These 9 documents were added to the 21 documents previously included, for complete review in the next stage.

In the fourth stage of full-text revision, out of the 30 documents considered, three were excluded as they did not meet the inclusion criteria. Specifically, the documents dealt exclusively with quantitative aspects of meta-analysis and not with software features related to SLR. Prior to the work of analysis, the administrator manually uploaded all 27 documents on PDF format and assigned each document to a specific canonical document. It is important to note that only the administrator and the analysts have access to the PDFs assigned for review. If the same canonical document is used in another review, only the metadata will be shared.

The analyst used the form created in the first stage to extract information from the 27 included documents. As seen on Fig. 4, the full-text revision interface shows the PDF file for the document, the form for extracting information from the document, and the

decision interface, which is similar to the one used in the screening stages. It should be noted that live codes can be used in the form fields, placing the code inside brackets, later be summarized in the reporting stage.

Finally, there are three available reports in the reporting stage. A PRISMA flow diagram (Fig. 5) is available, that can provide a summary of the documents that were included and excluded at each stage of the systematic review. A process report can also be retrieved, in the form of a web page or an Excel file, that shows all of the analysts’ decisions and the resolutions adopted by the administrator. Both PRISMA and the process reports give an account of the inclusion and exclusion of documents. The information extraction report shows the information for all fields completed in full by each analyst, and also summarizes live codes, showing how many were used and the paragraph that each was collected from.

docs.title: 5.2. Backward snowballing and automation of Buhos
docs.text:
One of the most important functionalities of Buhos is its capacity to perform backward snowballing, i.e., to search for common references within a set of selected documents.

To exemplify, a search was done of tertiary studies (systematic reviews of systematic reviews) on Software Engineering and Global Software Engineering. A search was performed in the Scopus databases (19 records), Web of Science (8 records) y IEEE (5 records) using similar search criteria. Following the deduplication process, 24 different documents were identified, of which 21 were accepted in the title and abstract screening. After incorporating the references of these documents using Crossref, Buhos was able to identify 26 documents that had been cited 2 or more times in the documents selected during the title and abstract screening stage.

In the /spec/watir/backward_snowballing.rb route of the source code the procedure previously shown is automatically replicated using watir. The screencast is available as Video 2.

docs.title: 6. Conclusions
docs.text:
This paper presents Buhos, a web-based systematic literature software that supplies the necessary functionalities for managing the complete literature review process, covering the stages of searching, screening, data extraction and reporting. The performance of rigorous systematic summaries, developed in the most efficient way possible, allows greater development in various scientific areas, as the preceding literature is better integrated into the new findings. The use of software allows researchers to track their decisions and disagreements, an extremely cumbersome process when performed manually. And because Buhos can be used in a distributed manner in multiple languages, systematic reviews can be carried out by multiple researchers working in conjunction from their respective countries. This would be particularly useful in SE, for teams developing SLR running Global Software Development. In the case of Social Sciences, using international work teams would avoid bias associated with language or cultural position, a significant factor for ensuring the validity of results in this field of knowledge [107].

During the development period, the software was integrated in a natural manner to the workflow of various researchers, who remarked on the improved organization of their work and how the software’s capability for analyzing citation relationships between articles greatly facilitated gaining new insights into the literature. Specifically, the software is being used by five doctoral students of Psychology in Chile’s University of Concepción who are simultaneously conducting online systematic reviews. The most advanced of these is a systematic review on the crisis of replicability in social psychology, coordinating the work of four reviewers.

docs.title: Online tools supporting the conduct and reporting of systematic reviews and systematic maps: a case study on CADIMA and review of existing tools
docs.text: Christian Kohl1*† , Emma J. McIntosh2† , Stefan Unger1† , Neal R. Haddaway3 , Steffen Kecke1 , Joachim Schiemann1 and Ralf Wilhelm1

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text:
Systematic reviews and systematic maps represent powerful tools to identify, collect, evaluate and summarise primary research pertinent to a specific research question or topic in a highly standardised and reproducible manner. Even though they are seen as the “gold standard” when synthesising primary research, systematic reviews and maps are typically resource-intensive and complex activities. Thus, managing the conduct and reporting of such reviews can become a time consuming and challenging task. This paper introduces the open access online tool CADIMA, which was developed through a collaboration between the Julius Kühn-Institut and the Collaboration for Environmental Evidence, in order to increase the efficiency of the evidence synthesis process and facilitate reporting of all activities to maximise methodological rigour. Furthermore, we analyse how CADIMA compares with other available tools by providing a comprehensive summary of existing software designed for the purposes of systematic review management. We show that CADIMA is the only available open access tool that is designed to: (1) assist throughout the systematic review/map process; (2) be suited to reviews broader than medical sciences; (3) allow for offline data extraction; and, (4) support working as a review team.

Keywords: Review management, Managing systems, Systematic review software, Evidence synthesis, Time management, Rapid review, Text mining

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Systematic reviews were first established in the field of healthcare to support evidence-based decision making [1]. Their use is continuously expanding into other disciplines, including social welfare, international development, education, crime and justice,1 environmental management2 (including the impact assessment of crop genetic improvement technologies [2–4]), software engineering [5] and food/feed safety assessment [6].

*Correspondence: christian.kohl@julius-kuehn.de

Systematic reviews and related systematic maps follow standardised and rigorous methodologies aiming to ensure comprehensiveness, minimise bias, and increase transparency [7, 8]. Although seen as a “gold standard” when synthesising primary research, the central tenets of systematic review and map methodologies necessarily increase the complexity of the review processes and their resource requirements (i.e. time, money and personnel).

In order to support reviewers throughout the conduct of their syntheses, and to increase efficiency and maximise methodological rigour, software tools have been developed by a diverse set of providers to support review
